elements.text:
Case Study 1 - Anna (late teens)

Anna is a 19-year-old woman who has always tried to live up to high expectations - both her own and those of her family and friends. On the outside, Anna seems confident and successful: she excelled at school, earning top grades, and secured a place to study medicine at a good university. Her future looks bright, and everyone around her tells her so. She is well-liked by her peers, and stays involved in her church - she is an active member of the church band, and also helps to organise teens events. To others, she seems to be thriving - a picture of success, confidence, and balance.

But beneath the surface, Anna is wrestling with inner turmoil. She feels like she’s constantly switching between two extremes. At times, after receiving praise from a teacher or finishing a challenging assignment, she feels proud of her accomplishments and tells herself that she’s on the right track. But these moments don’t last. Other times, especially if anything goes wrong, she feels like a fraud, doubting her abilities and feeling crushed by the fear that she’ll never measure up.

This inner tension is exhausting for Anna. When she looks at others, she either compares herself favourably and feels pride, or she feels inadequate and spirals into insecurity and anxiety. She’s not sure who she really is, and she’s starting to wonder if she will know. Recently, Anna has been praying about her identity, asking God to help her understand herself more clearly. But she still struggles with feelings of confusion, not knowing how to reconcile her strengths and weaknesses. She has also begun avoiding deep conversations with her family and friends, fearful that if she opens up about her struggles, they’ll be disappointed in her or see her as weak.

Anna wonders: ‘How do I truly understand myself? Will I ever find peace, or will I always be torn between extremes?’ She longs for clarity, but she feels trapped in a cycle of confusion, pride, self-doubt, and anxiety.

“We are not very good at recognizing illusions, least of all the ones we cherish about ourselves - the ones we are born with and which feed the roots of sin.”
Thomas Merton

“The more we try to understand ourselves, the more lost we get. True freedom is not in figuring out who we are, but in forgetting ourselves and looking to Christ.”
Tim Keller

“Man is neither angel nor beast, and unhappily whoever wants to act the angel, acts the beast.”
Blaise Pascal

“We do not know ourselves until we have learned to look at ourselves from God’s perspective. We are strangers to our own hearts.”
C.S. Lewis

elements.text: Human beings are a conundrum, wrapped up in a paradox, inside a mystery. We are capable of boundless goodness and endless evil, tremendous heights and horrendous depths. We are finite, yet God-imaging; good, yet fallen; great, yet wretched. It is difficult to understand us as a group, or any one of us as an individual.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> The human mind is more deceitful than anything else. It is incurably bad. Who can understand it?

elements.question: Why is it hard to understand ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jeremiah doesn't just say the mind is unreliable — he says it is 'deceitful' and 'incurably bad,' which means the very instrument we'd use to examine ourselves is the thing that's compromised. That's why the verse ends with a question rather than an answer: 'Who can understand it?' It isn't rhetorical throat-clearing — it's an honest admission that self-knowledge has a built-in blind spot. We can't fully trust our own read on ourselves, because the mind doing the reading is the same mind capable of deceiving us. That's a humbling starting point for any study on identity: some outside light is going to be necessary.
elements.questionHint: The verse calls the mind 'deceitful' — if the thing doing the self-examining is itself untrustworthy, what problem does that create for figuring yourself out from the inside alone?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For I don’t understand what I am doing. For I do not do what I want – instead, I do what I hate.  <sup>16</sup> But if I do what I don’t want, I agree that the law is good.  <sup>17</sup> But now it is no longer me doing it, but sin that lives in me. <sup>18</sup> For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For I want to do the good, but I cannot do it.  <sup>19</sup> For I do not do the good I want, but I do the very evil I do not want!

elements.question: Why are we sometimes confused about what we do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes a strange split: 'I do not do what I want – instead, I do what I hate.' He isn't confused about right and wrong in the abstract; he's confused about why his actions don't match his own desires. His explanation is that 'it is no longer me doing it, but sin that lives in me' — as if something foreign has taken up residence inside him and is pulling against his own will. That's disorienting because it means self-understanding isn't just a matter of figuring out what you want; even when you know what you want, something in you resists it, which makes 'who I am' feel divided rather than simple.
elements.questionHint: Paul says it's 'no longer me doing it, but sin that lives in me' — what does it mean for someone to feel like there are two different wills operating inside the same person?

elements.text: As fallen creatures, our view of simple things within the world can easily be distorted; our view of ourselves can especially easily be distorted. We can be blinded by pride, so that we overestimate our goodness, power, and abilities.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>Jesus also told this parable to some who were confident that they were righteous and looked down on everyone else. <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.  <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee stood and prayed about himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people: extortionists, unrighteous people, adulterers – or even like this tax collector.  <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I get.’

elements.question: Why can looking at others sometimes hinder self-understanding?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Pharisee's prayer is really a report card measured against other people: 'I thank you that I am not like other people' — and he names the worst examples he can think of, then lists his own religious achievements. He isn't examining himself at all; he's scanning the room for someone to look worse than. That's the trap — comparison lets you feel secure without ever actually looking inward, because your standard becomes 'better than them' instead of anything true about your own heart. Looking down on someone else can feel like self-knowledge, but it's really just a way of avoiding it.
elements.questionHint: The Pharisee measures himself by saying he's not 'like other people' — what does he never actually stop to look at when comparison is doing all the work?

elements.text: We can always find someone ’worse’ to compare ourselves with, so that we feel we are a much better person. Or we can be blinded by anxiety (or even despair), so that we underestimate our goodness, power, and abilities. We can always find someone ’better’ to compare ourselves with, so that we feel we are a much worse person.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but fail to see the beam of wood in your own? <sup>4</sup> Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while there is a beam in your own? <sup>5</sup> You hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

elements.question: How else do we sometimes hinder self-understanding?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus paints a deliberately absurd picture: someone fussing over a 'speck' in another person's eye while there's a 'beam of wood' lodged in his own. The size difference is the whole point — it's not that we notice others' faults and ignore ours equally, it's that our own faults are often bigger and we still see them as smaller. He calls this pattern hypocrisy because it lets a person appear helpful and discerning about others while staying blind about themselves. Real self-understanding, according to Jesus, has to start with dealing with your own beam before you're qualified to comment on anyone's speck.
elements.questionHint: Jesus contrasts a tiny 'speck' with a 'beam of wood' — why would he pick such an exaggerated size difference to describe how we see other people's faults versus our own?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> For if someone merely listens to the message and does not live it out, he is like someone who gazes at his own face in a mirror. <sup>24</sup> For he gazes at himself and then goes out and immediately forgets what sort of person he was.

elements.question: How else do we sometimes hinder self-understanding?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James compares hearing God's word without living it to glancing in a mirror and then walking away having 'immediately' forgotten your own face. That's an odd kind of forgetting — you'd think seeing yourself clearly would stick. But James's point is that hearing truth without acting on it doesn't actually change your self-perception; it evaporates the moment you stop looking. So merely listening — nodding along, feeling convicted in the moment — isn't the same as knowing yourself. Real self-understanding requires that what you see gets carried out the door and lived, or the reflection never actually becomes knowledge.
elements.questionHint: James says the man 'immediately forgets what sort of person he was' right after looking in the mirror — what does that forgetting suggest is missing besides just looking?

elements.passageText:
12 There is a way that seems right to a person,
but its end is the way that leads to death.

elements.question: How else do we sometimes hinder self-understanding?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb's warning is packed into one word: 'seems.' A way can feel entirely right — confident, reasonable, justified — and still end in death. That gap between how something seems and where it actually leads is exactly what makes self-deception dangerous: it doesn't feel like deception from the inside. If our own sense of rightness were a reliable guide, this proverb wouldn't need to exist. It's a caution against trusting your own certainty as proof of truth, because certainty and correctness aren't the same thing, and by the time the end reveals itself, the way has already been walked.
elements.questionHint: The proverb says the way only 'seems right' — what does that word admit about the difference between how confident something feels and where it actually leads?

elements.text: Our sense of self can flip between extremes - the gloriously angelic, and the hideously bestial. There is a cure for this confusion: we must know God in order to truly know ourselves. We must know that He is our Creator. When we consider his holiness and glory, it puts our own self-aggrandising tendencies in perspective. When we consider his love for us it banishes our self-loathing tendencies.

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Examine me, and probe my thoughts! Test me, and know my concerns! See if there is any idolatrous tendency in me, and lead me in the reliable ancient path!

elements.question: How can knowing God help us understand ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Notice who David asks to do the searching: not himself, but God — 'Examine me, and probe my thoughts! Test me, and know my concerns!' Given how deceitful our own minds can be, this is the logical move: if you can't fully trust your own self-assessment, you invite someone who can see truly to do it for you. David isn't afraid of what might be found — he specifically asks God to check for 'idolatrous tendency,' the kind of misplaced allegiance a person might not even notice in themselves. Knowing God well enough to trust him with that search is what makes real self-understanding possible.
elements.questionHint: David doesn't examine himself — he asks God to 'examine me' and 'probe my thoughts.' Why would inviting someone else to search you succeed where searching yourself might fail?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> He says, “Stop your striving and recognize that I am God! I will be exalted over the nations! I will be exalted over the earth!” <sup>11</sup> The Lord who commands armies is on our side! The God of Jacob is our protector! (Selah)

elements.question: How can knowing God help us understand ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's command here is surprisingly simple: 'Stop your striving and recognize that I am God!' Self-understanding, in this psalm, doesn't come from more analysis or effort — it comes from stillness in front of someone bigger than you. Once you recognize who God actually is — exalted over the nations and the earth, the one 'on our side,' our protector — your own size and situation come into focus by comparison. You see yourself rightly not by staring harder at yourself, but by looking at him and realizing you're small, dependent, and, remarkably, defended by someone far greater than any threat you face.
elements.questionHint: God says 'stop your striving' before 'recognize that I am God' — why would ceasing effort, rather than trying harder, be the doorway to recognizing something true?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> (See what sort of love the Father has given to us: that we should be called God’s children – and indeed we are! For this reason the world does not know us: because it did not know him.

elements.question: How can knowing God help us understand ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John doesn't just state a fact, he marvels at it — 'see what sort of love' — and then adds an exclamation most translations soften but the text clearly carries: 'and indeed we are!' That extra emphasis matters, because it answers a doubt before it's even raised: this isn't a title we've earned or a status that might be revoked, it's a settled reality given entirely by the Father's love. Knowing that God is the kind of God who calls people his children reframes the question 'who am I?' — the answer isn't found by digging into yourself, but by receiving what he's already declared.
elements.questionHint: John doesn't just say we're called children — he adds 'and indeed we are!' What is that extra emphasis meant to settle for someone who might doubt it?

elements.text: Knowing that God is our Creator, and that we are his creatures, is ’square one’ when it comes to knowledge of ourselves. There are many more squares to go.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> Counsel in a person’s heart is like deep water, but an understanding person draws it out.

elements.question: What warning, and encouragement, do Proverbs give us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb pictures what's inside a person as 'deep water' — not shallow or immediately visible, but something you have to work to reach. That's the warning: don't assume you already know your own heart just because it's yours; it takes real effort to get down to it. But the proverb also holds out encouragement, because it says an 'understanding person draws it out' — meaning that depth isn't unreachable, just resistant to a quick glance. With patience, wisdom, and probably help from someone who knows how to ask the right questions, what's hidden in us can actually be brought up into the light.
elements.questionHint: The proverb calls inner counsel 'deep water' that has to be 'drawn out' — what does drawing water up from a well require that a quick glance at the surface doesn't?

elements.text:
Case Study 1b - Anna shaped by truth

The enigma of the heart - including its deceitfulness - explains why it is so hard for Anna to see herself clearly. When she compares herself to others, her heart tricks her into either feeling prideful or insecure, depending on whom she’s comparing herself to. But Anna’s identity cannot be found by measuring herself against others. As she learns to step away from these comparisons, she will begin to see herself more clearly - not through the lens of human standards, but through God’s eyes.

Anna’s turning point will come when she realizes that true self-understanding comes from knowing God. It is as we ask God to search our hearts and reveal the truth that we can begin to understand who we really are. Anna needs to stop relying on her own assessment and start relying on God’s view of her.

God created Anna and knows her intimately. He sees both her strengths and her weaknesses and loves her deeply, not because of what she has achieved but because she is His child. By focusing on who God is and how He sees her, Anna can find the peace she has been searching for. She doesn’t need to live in the tension between pride and insecurity - she can rest in the knowledge that her identity is secure in Christ.

As Anna learns to look to Christ for her identity, she will begin to understand herself in a new way. Instead of fixating on her achievements or failures, she can focus on Christ’s love, grace, and sacrifice.

Anna’s feelings of confusion and frustration are normal for a believer, but they don’t define her. By turning to Christ, she can find the strength to overcome the battle within herself and live in the freedom that comes from being made new in Him.

For Anna, the path forward involves regularly seeking God’s perspective on her life. Replacing her thoughts of pride or insecurity with biblical truth will help her see herself more clearly. She can spend time asking God to reveal any areas where her view of herself is distorted. Anna can invite trusted friends or mentors to speak truth into her life, helping her discern areas where she may be blind to her strengths or weaknesses.

chapters.chapterTitle: Created in the Image of God

elements.text:
Case Study 2 - Mark (late-20s)

Mark is a 29-year-old software engineer who has always been a high achiever. He began his career straight out of college, landing a good job at a fast-growing tech company. Over the years, he worked long hours, tackled difficult projects, and consistently delivered results. His dedication paid off as he quickly climbed the ranks, earning praise from his supervisors and becoming known as the go-to person for complex problems.

But as time has gone by, Mark’s sense of self-worth began to shift. He always took pride in his skills and achievements, but recently he has started to depend more and more on his performance at work. Every successful project makes him feel validated and important. But if he fails at a project - or even if he succeeds, but his contributions aren’t particularly recognised or celebrated - he feels like a failure, and starts to doubt himself.

Recently, Mark experienced a major setback. He had been eyeing a promotion that he believed he was more than qualified for. He had worked tirelessly for months, hoping his efforts would secure him the promotion. But when the announcement came, the position was given to someone else - a colleague whom Mark considered less capable and less hard-working. The news shook him to his core. He felt frustrated, undervalued and also deeply insecure. He began to question whether he was as good as he thought and whether his hard work had even been worth it.

Mark also struggles with seeing the value in others, especially those he thinks are less talented, or less successful, or less driven. He finds himself becoming critical of coworkers who don’t put in the same effort he does, and he has a hard time showing kindness to people who seem to ’get in the way’ of his progress. In his quieter moments, Mark realises he’s measuring himself and others by the wrong standards, but he’s not sure how to stop.

Mark asks himself: ‘If I’m not successful or recognized for my hard work, what’s my real worth?’ He also wonders how can he learn to see value in others when they seem to fall so short so often.

You created us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless
until they rest in You.
Augustine

Man is neither angel nor beast
Blaise Pascal

People travel to wonder at the height of the mountains, at the huge waves of the seas, at the long course of the rivers, at the vast compass of the ocean, at the circular motion of the stars, and yet they pass by the mystery of themselves without wondering.
Augustine

elements.text: Being God’s image implies many great and glorious things. But it is worth beginning by reminding ourselves that it also implies some more humbling things. It means we are derivative, not original. God is the original masterpiece, we are the images, the miniature reproductions. And because we are derivative, it is no surprise to find out that we are dependant. God is the only one who is totally self-sufficient. We, however, depend on his generosity.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, so they may rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the cattle, over all the earth, and over all the creatures that move on the earth.” <sup>27</sup> God created humankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them, male and female he created them.

elements.question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse doesn't leave 'image' and 'likeness' as abstract ideas — it immediately attaches a purpose to them: 'so they may rule.' Being made like God is tied to being given real responsibility to govern creation on his behalf, the way a representative reflects the one who sent them. And it's explicit that this applies to everyone equally: 'male and female he created them' both bear the image, not one more than the other. So identity here isn't primarily about appearance or intellect — it's about being God's appointed representatives, entrusted with a role that mirrors his own care and authority over the world.
elements.questionHint: The command to rule comes right after 'in our image, after our likeness' — what does attaching a job to the image suggest about what bearing it actually means?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Of what importance is the human race, that you should notice them? Of what importance is mankind, that you should pay attention to them, <sup>5</sup> and make them a little less than the heavenly beings? You grant mankind honor and majesty; <sup>6</sup> you appoint them to rule over your creation; you have placed everything under their authority,

elements.question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm opens in genuine wonder — 'of what importance is the human race, that you should notice them?' — as if the psalmist can hardly believe the answer he's about to give. That answer is startling: humanity is made 'a little less than the heavenly beings,' crowned with 'honor and majesty,' and appointed to rule over creation with 'everything... placed under their authority.' This isn't humanity claiming greatness for itself; it's God's own assessment of the rank he's given us, positioned just under the heavenly realm and set in charge of the earth. Being made in God's image means carrying dignity and delegated authority we didn't invent for ourselves.
elements.questionHint: The psalm says humanity is made 'a little less than the heavenly beings' — what rank is being given here, and who decided it?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people made in God’s image.

elements.question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James zeroes in on something practical: the same tongue that blesses 'the Lord and Father' can turn around and curse 'people made in God's image.' By putting those two acts side by side, he makes cursing another person more than rudeness — it's an offense against the image God stamped on them. This matters for identity because it means every person you meet, however unimpressive or difficult, carries something of God's own likeness. You can't genuinely honor God while treating his image-bearers with contempt; the two are inseparably connected, which is exactly why James finds the contradiction so glaring.
elements.questionHint: James points out it's 'with it' — the same tongue — doing both the blessing and the cursing. What does using one instrument for such opposite purposes reveal?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> For a man should not have his head covered, since he is the image and glory of God. But the woman is the glory of the man.

elements.question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse uses the word 'image' more narrowly than Genesis does — it's part of Paul's argument about head coverings and order in Corinthian worship, not a full statement on who bears God's image. Here he calls the man 'the image and glory of God' and the woman 'the glory of the man,' framing image and glory as relational: something reflected outward within a relationship, not just an individual possession. It's a reminder that Scripture uses this language with some nuance depending on context — earlier we saw that both male and female together bear God's image in Genesis; here Paul is drawing out a specific relational dimension of glory within his own argument.
elements.questionHint: Paul pairs 'image' here with the word 'glory' rather than leaving it alone — what does adding 'glory' suggest about a relational, not just individual, dimension to this verse?

elements.text: In the language of Pascal, human beings are neither beasts nor angels (nor gods). We are linked with, yet distinguished from, the animals: we are created on Day 6 like them, and we are formed from ’the dust’ like them; yet we alone are said to be the image of God, and we alone are placed in a position of authority over the rest of creation.

elements.passageText: <sup>28</sup> God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply! Fill the earth and subdue it! Rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that moves on the ground.” <sup>29</sup> Then God said, “I now give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the entire earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food. <sup>30</sup> And to all the animals of the earth, and to every bird of the air, and to all the creatures that move on the ground – everything that has the breath of life in it – I give every green plant for food.” It was so. <sup>31</sup> God saw all that he had made – and it was very good! There was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day.

elements.question: What was God’s original plan for humanity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's blessing comes packed with active verbs: 'be fruitful and multiply,' 'fill the earth,' 'subdue it,' 'rule.' None of these describe passive existence — they describe a calling to grow, spread, cultivate, and govern. Alongside that, he generously provides for every need: 'every seed-bearing plant' and 'every tree that has fruit' are given for food, with no hint of scarcity. And the whole scene is capped with God's own verdict: 'it was very good.' God's original plan wasn't just for humanity to survive in the world he made — it was for them to actively multiply, steward, and enjoy it under his blessing.
elements.questionHint: God stacks up 'fill... subdue... rule' as one blessing — what do those three commands have in common about the kind of life humanity was meant to have?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> The Lord God took the man and placed him in the orchard in Eden to care for it and to maintain it. <sup>16</sup> Then the Lord God commanded the man, “You may freely eat fruit from every tree of the orchard, <sup>17</sup> but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will surely die.”

elements.question: What was God’s original plan for humanity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God places the man in the orchard with a job — 'to care for it and to maintain it' — meaning purposeful work was part of the plan from the very beginning, not a punishment added later. Then comes remarkable freedom: 'you may freely eat fruit from every tree,' with only a single exception named. The plan wasn't restriction; it was abundance bounded by one clear line, given with a real warning attached to it. God's design combined meaningful responsibility, generous provision, and a boundary meant to be trusted rather than second-guessed — all three together, not one without the others.
elements.questionHint: Before naming the one restriction, God says the man may 'freely eat fruit from every tree' — how much freedom actually surrounded that single boundary?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> He has told you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord really wants from you: He wants you to promote justice, to be faithful, and to live obediently before your God.

elements.question: What was God’s original plan for humanity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah names three things God wants, and none of them are ritual performances: 'promote justice, be faithful, and live obediently before your God.' That's a picture of character and relationship rather than a checklist of religious tasks. Justice points outward, toward how we treat others fairly; faithfulness points toward steady, trustworthy commitment; and living obediently before God points toward an ongoing posture, not a one-time achievement. Together they describe humanity's original calling as something relational and moral at its core — not primarily about what we produce or accomplish, but about the kind of people we become in how we treat God and others.
elements.questionHint: Micah names justice, faithfulness, and walking obediently together as one answer — what kind of life do those three things describe when held together rather than separately?

elements.text: The image of God is not shared by any animal, nor anything else in all creation, not even the angels. Humanity is the image of God (1 Corinthians 11:7). The emphasis falls not on one aspect of our constitution (e.g. rationality, or spirituality) but on who we are, and the situation in which God has put us, and the role he has given us. We are defined in relationship to God. We are the created representation of the Creator; we are the concrete manifestation of his glory here on earth.

elements.question: What is unusual about the pronouns God uses for Himself?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God says, 'Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness' — plural pronouns from the one God who has no other gods beside him. That's genuinely strange if God were simply a solitary individual; there'd be no one else to include in 'us' and 'our.' The unusual pronoun hints that something communal or relational exists within God's own being, even before he creates anyone else. And if humanity is made in the image of a God who is inherently relational, it starts to explain why we, too, are built for relationship rather than designed to thrive in isolation.
elements.questionHint: God says 'let us make... in our image' while remaining one God — who else could that plural 'us' possibly be including?

elements.text: When God announces his intention to create humanity, He says ’Let us make’ - which suggests plurality and relationship within God Himself. Relationship is built on the plurality of, and distinction between, people. Relationship is fundamental to who God is, and now it is being made fundamental to who human beings are. Relationship is built into us from the very moment of our creation - indeed, from the very moment of our conception in the mind of God. Relationships are not an accidental extra, added to creation as an afterthought. They are at the heart of reality, at the centre of who God is, and core to who humans are.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> The Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a companion for him who corresponds to him.”

elements.question: What is the one thing in Genesis 1-2 that is not good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Everything else in Genesis 1 gets called 'good' or 'very good,' which makes this line stand out sharply: 'It is not good for the man to be alone.' In a chapter full of divine approval, this is the one thing God himself flags as deficient — not sin, not failure, just solitude itself. And notice what God proposes isn't merely company but 'a companion for him who corresponds to him' — someone genuinely matched to him, not just present alongside him. Even before anything had gone wrong, God built humanity for relationship that fits, not for isolated self-sufficiency.
elements.questionHint: God doesn't just promise the man company — he promises 'a companion... who corresponds to him.' What kind of companion is being described there, beyond simply 'someone'?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> Two people are better than one, because they can reap more benefit from their labor. <sup>10</sup> For if they fall, one will help his companion up, but pity the person who falls down and has no one to help him up.

elements.question: Why do we not function well alone?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Preacher makes his case with a very concrete picture: 'if they fall, one will help his companion up, but pity the person who falls down and has no one to help him up.' It's not an abstract claim about companionship being nice — it's about what happens specifically in a moment of weakness or failure. Alone, a fall just stays a fall; with someone else, it becomes recoverable. That's the practical reason isolation doesn't work well for us: we're not just less efficient alone, as the 'more benefit from labor' also shows, we're also more exposed when things go wrong and there's no one there to lift us back up.
elements.questionHint: The passage pictures someone falling with 'no one to help him up' — what specific vulnerability does that scenario expose that working alone might otherwise hide?

elements.text: Even before the Fall humans needed community. We were not made to be alone; we are created with a need for companionship. The creation of Eve is the beginning of marriage, and of friendship, of family, and of community. Community is built into the image of God from the very beginning. We are most truly God’s image not in splendid isolation, but when we love one another.

elements.text:
Case Study 2b - Mark and the image of God

Mark’s struggle with his self-worth stems from a misunderstanding of where his value truly lies. He has been measuring his worth based on his performance and success at work. But our worth comes from the fact that we are created in the image of God. This means that Mark’s value is not dependent on his achievements - it is inherent in who he already is, because God made him. He doesn’t need to earn his worth - it was given to him by his Creator. By understanding this, Mark can begin to let go of the pressure to constantly prove himself and find peace in the knowledge that he is already valuable in God’s eyes.

Mark will also find it easier to see value in others if he can fully take on board the truth that we are all made in the image of God. Every person, regardless of their achievements or failures, is made in God’s likeness. For Mark, this means that even those coworkers he finds frustrating or less capable are still worthy of respect and love because they, too, bear God’s image. If Mark can start to see others as God sees them, he will be able to show more grace, kindness, and understanding. Instead of measuring people by this world’s standards of success, he can learn to value them as God’s creations, just as he values himself.

Being made in the image of God means being dependent on Him. We are not self-sufficient - we are derivative, reflecting God’s glory. Mark’s desire for recognition and success may well stem from a desire to be self-sufficient, to prove his worth without relying on anyone else - not even God. But God created us to do great things as we depend on Him. He didn’t create us to strive for independence. If Mark can accept his dependency on God’s grace and provision, he will find freedom from the constant pressure to perform. Instead of trying to prove himself through his work, Mark can focus on reflecting God’s character in how he treats others, finding purpose in that reflection rather than in recognition by the world.

We were created for community. Mark’s drive for success has led him to isolate himself from others, viewing them as competition rather than companions. But recognising that relationships are central to being made in God’s image will help Mark build healthier connections with those around him. By valuing relationships and teamwork, Mark can begin to foster a community that reflects God’s love and unity. This shift in perspective will not only enrich Mark’s own life but also benefit those he works with, as he starts to see them as partners rather than obstacles.

Case Study 3 - Sarah (late-30s)

Sarah is a 37-year-old Christian who loves God and has been following Christ faithfully for years. She is active in her church, leads a small group, and often encourages others in their faith. From the outside she shows many signs of spiritual maturity - she is someone others look up to for guidance and wisdom. But despite this, internally Sarah struggles deeply with feelings of guilt and shame over her past mistakes. She constantly feels as though she’s not good enough for God’s love. She knows, intellectually, that she’s forgiven through Christ. But so often in practice she finds herself feeling like her sins and mistakes define her.

Sarah often finds herself caught in a cycle of sin and repentance. She confesses her sins, feels forgiven for a short time, but soon after falls back into old habits of anger, jealousy, and impatience. Each time she stumbles, the weight of guilt grows heavier, and she starts to believe that God must be fed up with her. Sarah is afraid that she’ll never escape this cycle and wonders if she’s truly changed at all.

She was listening to a sermon once, and the preacher got people to imagine that God had appeared to them visibly, and that He was looking at them. The preacher then asked, ‘What expression would you expect to see on God’s face? What expression would be in his eyes as he looks at you?’

As soon as Sarah heard the question, she knew what expression she would see in God’s eyes: disappointment. She could almost picture the look of disapproval she believed God would have as He saw her struggles and shortcomings. It was the expression of someone who had given countless chances, only to be let down again and again.

This moment lingered in Sarah’s mind long after the sermon ended. Since then, she has started asking herself these questions: ‘If I’m really forgiven, why do I still feel so guilty? Why does sin still have such a strong grip on me, even though I’ve been a Christian for so long?’

She doesn’t have an answer.

As the salt flavours every drop in the Atlantic, so does sin affect every atom of our nature. It is so sadly there, so abundantly there, that if you cannot detect it, you are deceived.
Charles Spurgeon

My sin was this, that I looked for pleasure, beauty, and truth not in Him but in myself and His other creatures, and the search led me instead to pain, confusion, and error.
Augustine

elements.text: The serpent appears unannounced in Genesis 3, and quickly demonstrates a master-class of deception. He begins, not with an out-right lie, but with an insidious question: ‘Did God really say ... ?’

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now the serpent was more shrewd than any of the wild animals that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Is it really true that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the orchard’?”

elements.question: How does the serpent distort what God has said?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Compare the serpent's question to what God actually said back in the garden: God had told the man he could 'freely eat fruit from every tree,' with only one exception. The serpent flips that entirely, asking, 'Is it really true that God said, “You must not eat from any tree of the orchard”?' — turning one narrow restriction into a total ban. That distortion makes God sound stingy and controlling rather than generous, and it's delivered as an innocent-sounding question rather than a flat accusation, which makes it easier to plant doubt without directly attacking God. Exaggerating a limit into a prohibition is exactly how the serpent gets Eve second-guessing God's character.
elements.questionHint: The serpent says 'any tree' — but God's actual command allowed eating from every tree except one. What's the difference between those two versions of the rule?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit from the trees of the orchard; <sup>3</sup> but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the orchard God said, ‘You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or else you will die.’”

elements.question: Eve corrects the serpent incorrectly! What does she get wrong?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Eve rightly corrects the serpent's exaggeration by naming the actual tree, but then she overcorrects: she adds 'and you must not touch it,' a restriction God never gave. His original command was only about eating, with no mention of touching at all. By adding to what God said, she makes the command sound harsher and more arbitrary than it was — which, ironically, makes it easier for the serpent to later argue that touching the fruit does no harm, undermining a rule God never actually gave in the first place. Getting God's word slightly wrong, even while trying to defend it, left her more vulnerable, not less.
elements.questionHint: Eve adds 'and you must not touch it' — go back to God's actual command in Genesis 2:17. Does it say anything about touching?

elements.text: Eve adds to God’s command - God never said anything about touching the tree. But also, Genesis 2:9b tells us that there were two trees in the middle of the garden: ‘the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.’ Eve’s eye has already passed over the tree that she should be eating from - the tree of life! - and has focused, unhealthily, on the tree that she should be avoiding.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.    <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee stood and prayed about himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people: extortionists, unrighteous people, adulterers – or even like this tax collector.    <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I get.’ <sup>13</sup> The tax collector, however, stood far off and would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, be merciful to me, sinner that I am!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you that this man went down to his home justified rather than the Pharisee. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

elements.question: How can focusing on the wrong thing lead us into sin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The two men in the temple are focused on completely different things. The Pharisee's prayer is aimed at comparison — 'I thank you that I am not like other people' — and at his own résumé of fasting and tithing. The tax collector, by contrast, won't even 'look up to heaven' and focuses only on his own need: 'God, be merciful to me, sinner that I am!' Jesus says it's the second man who goes home justified. Focusing on how you measure up against others, or on your own accomplishments, keeps you from seeing your actual need before God — and Jesus's closing line makes the stakes plain: 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.'
elements.questionHint: One man prays 'I am not like other people,' the other prays 'be merciful to me, sinner that I am.' Where is each man's attention actually pointed?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But be careful that this liberty of yours does not become a hindrance to the weak.

elements.question: How can focusing on the wrong thing lead us into sin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's warning is short but pointed: something that's genuinely permissible for you — your 'liberty' — 'does not become a hindrance to the weak.' The word 'hindrance' is doing real work here: it means your freedom can become an obstacle that trips someone else up, even when nothing you did was technically wrong. Focusing only on what you're allowed to do, without asking who else is affected, can quietly turn a good freedom into a cause of someone else's sin. It's a reminder that self-focus — even self-focus on legitimate rights — can still lead toward harm if it ignores the people around you.
elements.questionHint: Paul warns that liberty can become a 'hindrance to the weak' — what does the word 'hindrance' suggest about who might get hurt by a freedom that's otherwise fine?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For when we were in the flesh, the sinful desires, aroused by the law, were active in the members of our body to bear fruit for death. <sup>6</sup> But now we have been released from the law, because we have died to what controlled us, so that we may serve in the new life of the Spirit and not under the old written code.

elements.question: How can focusing on the wrong thing lead us into sin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul makes a startling claim: sinful desires were 'aroused by the law' — meaning fixation on the rule itself, rather than curbing sin, actually stirred it up. Focusing on the law as the center of attention, rather than on God himself, produced 'fruit for death' instead of obedience. His solution isn't better rule-focus but a change of orientation entirely — being 'released from the law' and now serving 'in the new life of the Spirit and not under the old written code.' Where our attention lands shapes what grows in us; fixating on the letter of a rule can backfire in ways that trusting and following the Spirit doesn't.
elements.questionHint: Paul says sinful desires were 'aroused by the law' — what does it mean that focusing on the rule itself is described as stirring up the very thing it forbids?

elements.text: The serpent advances towards openly contradicting God, and makes three claims: (i) You will not surely die; (ii) your eyes will be opened; and (iii) you will be like God, knowing good and evil. He is implying that God is holding Adam and Eve back; that God does not have their best interests at heart; that God’s restrictions are not for their good; and their lives will be better if they rise above God’s restrictions, and seize control of their own destiny.

elements.passageText:
2 But your sinful acts have alienated you from your God;
your sins have caused him to reject you and not listen to your prayers.

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah doesn't soften the language: sin has 'alienated you from your God' and caused him to 'reject you and not listen to your prayers.' This isn't describing a vague feeling of guilt — it's describing real relational breakdown, the kind where communication itself stops working, like a friendship gone so cold that calls no longer get answered. Sin isn't presented here as a private failing that stays contained inside a person; it actively damages the relationship it's committed against, creating genuine distance between the sinner and God, distance that shows up concretely in prayers that seem to go unheard.
elements.questionHint: Isaiah says sin causes God to 'not listen to your prayers' — what everyday kind of relationship breakdown does that unanswered-communication picture resemble?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> If we say we have fellowship with him and yet keep on walking in the darkness, we are lying and not practicing the truth.

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John names a specific contradiction: someone can claim to 'have fellowship with him' while still 'walking in the darkness' — and John's verdict is blunt: 'we are lying and not practicing the truth.' The lie isn't necessarily spoken to other people; it's a self-deception, a claim to closeness with God that the person's own ongoing life contradicts. This shows sin doesn't just create distance from God in some abstract sense — it makes our own claims about our relationship with him false in practice, no matter how sincerely we might say them, if the walking doesn't match the words.
elements.questionHint: John says persisting in darkness while claiming fellowship makes 'we are lying' — lying to whom, exactly, when the claim and the behavior don't match?

elements.text: The serpent’s claims are superficially ’true’ yet also devastatingly false. Adam and Eve are (i) still alive (i.e. not ’surely dead’); (ii) the ’eyes of both of them were opened’; and (iii) God declares, ‘The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil’. But the temptation implied seizing control of their destiny would make life much better for them. The way it turns out things are so much worse.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> The earth is defiled by its inhabitants, for they have violated laws, disregarded the regulation, and broken the permanent treaty. <sup>6</sup> So a treaty curse devours the earth; its inhabitants pay for their guilt. This is why the inhabitants of the earth disappear, and are reduced to just a handful of people.

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with the rest of creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah widens the lens beyond individual guilt: 'the earth is defiled by its inhabitants,' because people have 'violated laws' and 'broken the permanent treaty.' The consequence isn't confined to the people who sinned either — 'a treaty curse devours the earth' itself, and the land's inhabitants are reduced to 'just a handful.' Sin here isn't a private transaction between a person and God; it pollutes the shared world those people live in, and the created order itself absorbs and shows the damage of human unfaithfulness, far beyond whoever originally broke faith.
elements.questionHint: Isaiah says 'the earth is defiled by its inhabitants' — who does the defiling, and what ends up bearing the consequence alongside them?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> For the creation was subjected to futility – not willingly but because of God who subjected it – in hope <sup>21</sup> that the creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of decay into the glorious freedom of God’s children. <sup>22</sup> For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers together until now.

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with the rest of creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says creation itself was 'subjected to futility' — not by its own choice, but because of humanity's fall — and as a result 'the whole creation groans and suffers together until now.' That's a striking image: the natural world isn't neutral background to human sin, it's caught up in the same 'bondage of decay' that sin introduced. But the passage doesn't end in despair; it's framed by hope — creation waits to 'be set free... into the glorious freedom of God's children,' the same freedom promised to us. Sin bound creation to us in its groaning, and it's bound to us in its hoped-for release too.
elements.questionHint: Paul says creation 'groans' but does so 'in hope' — hope of what, according to the passage's own words about being 'set free'?

elements.text: Adam and Eve move from being at home in the garden, to exile outside it; from fellowship with God to exclusion; from honour to shame; from innocence to guilt; from security to fear; from blessing to curse; and from the sphere of life to the sphere of death.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> My whole body is sick because of your judgment; I am deprived of health because of my sin. <sup>4</sup> For my sins overwhelm me; like a heavy load, they are too much for me to bear.”

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with ourself?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist doesn't describe sin as merely a spiritual issue — he feels it physically: 'my whole body is sick because of your judgment,' and 'I am deprived of health because of my sin.' Then he shifts to the weight of it: his sins 'overwhelm me; like a heavy load, they are too much for me to bear.' Sin, in this psalm, doesn't stay tidily contained to the soul — it presses in on the body and the emotions too, leaving a person genuinely worn down, not just guilty in the abstract but exhausted and unwell under the actual felt weight of it.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist says his 'whole body is sick' because of his sin — what does that tell you about whether sin's effects stay only 'spiritual' or spread further?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For I want to do the good, but I cannot do it.  <sup>19</sup> For I do not do the good I want, but I do the very evil I do not want!

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with ourself?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul lands on a painful admission: 'nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh,' and then describes the gap that creates — 'I want to do the good, but I cannot do it.' Wanting and doing have come apart from each other inside him, which means sin doesn't just affect his actions, it fractures his relationship with his own will. He can no longer simply trust his intentions to translate into his behavior; there's a resistance built in. That internal splitting — desiring one thing and doing another — is exactly what makes sin's damage to self-understanding so disorienting.
elements.questionHint: Paul says 'I want to do the good, but I cannot do it' — what does that gap between wanting and doing reveal about a person's relationship with themselves?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? <sup>25</sup> Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

elements.question: What hope is there?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's cry is raw — 'Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?' — and notice that the answer doesn't come from more effort or self-discipline. It comes as a gift: 'Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!' The hope here isn't that the inner struggle instantly disappears — Paul still admits he serves 'the law of sin' with his flesh even after this — but that rescue has been provided from outside himself, through Christ, rather than needing to be achieved by finally winning the internal battle on his own. Hope, in other words, is received, not manufactured.
elements.questionHint: Paul moves from 'who will rescue me?' straight to 'thanks be to God' — is the rescue he describes something he accomplishes, or something given to him?

elements.text:
Case Study 3b - Sarah

Sarah’s battle with guilt is an example of how sin distorts our view of ourselves and our relationship with God. Sin creates a separation between us and God, and Sarah feels this separation sharply. That’s why she struggles with guilt even after confessing her sins. But it’s important for her to understand that this feeling of separation is not permanent. Sarah needs to recognise that sin affects every part of her being - her thoughts, emotions, and actions. But this awareness is not meant to drive her into despair; it’s meant to lead her to a deeper reliance on God’s grace.

The cycle of sin and guilt that Sarah experiences is part of the ongoing spiritual battle that every believer faces. But Sarah’s ongoing struggle with sin doesn’t negate the work of Christ - it highlights the very reason she needs Him. Sarah’s guilt deceives her into believing her sin is greater than God’s grace. That is not true. God’s grace is more powerful than her sin. When she repents, she is not trying to earn God’s favour - she is responding to the forgiveness that Christ has already provided on the cross. Sarah needs to hold on to this truth: God is transforming her, even in the midst of her struggles. Walking in the light of Christ means trusting His forgiveness and walking in truth, not in guilt. Sarah’s difficulty in accepting that she is forgiven reflects the deeper impact of sin on our relationship with ourselves. Sin causes us to believe lies about our worth and identity, convincing us that we are beyond hope. But as Sarah learns to embrace the truth of God’s grace, she will begin to see herself as God sees her - not with eyes of disappointment, but as eyes of delight. He sees her as his beloved child, forgiven and made new.

Sarah’s feelings of guilt do not define her. Her identity is found in Christ’s victory over sin. As she continues to seek God’s strength and rely on His grace, Sarah will see transformation in her life. She won’t experience immediate freedom from every sinful habit, but she can trust that God is at work within her, shaping her into the image of Christ. Each time she repents and returns to God, she is participating in the process of sanctification. Her battle is not in vain - it is part of the journey toward greater Christlikeness.

Sarah doesn’t need to remain trapped in the cycle of guilt and shame. If she embraces God’s grace, she can find freedom from the weight of sin, because it is already forgiven in Christ. This is the hope that she, and every believer, can hold onto as we navigate the tension between our fallen nature and our identity in Christ.

Case Study 4 - Michael (late 30s)

Michael is a Christian who has been active in his church for many years. He loves God, attends worship regularly, and serves on the church’s leadership team. But in the past few years, his career has begun to demand more and more of his time and attention. Michael is a manager at a growing tech company. He is good at his job, successful and ambitious, and he’s recently been offered a promotion that would increase his income and influence in the industry.

But Michael’s work has already taken a toll on his personal life. His wife, Rachel, has mentioned how much she misses spending time with him, and his children have become used to seeing him only briefly in the mornings before he rushes off to work. They are often in bed before he gets home. Michael’s involvement in church has also started to come under pressure - he’s often too tired or busy to attend Bible studies, he sometimes has to travel with work at weekends, and his prayer life has become more irregular.

Michael loves his family, and wants to see them do well in life. When Rachel has raised the issue of missing him, he has explained that all his hard work is for them, and for their progress. He believes that his career is part of God’s calling on his life. But he is beginning to feel that something is out of balance. Rachel recently confronted him more directly, saying, ‘I know you say you love us, but your actions are telling a different story. We don’t feel like we’re a priority any more.’

Michael is not sure what to do. He wonders: Can you love your family and God while also pursuing success at work? What does it mean to have a ’good balance’ when the demands of life pull you in many directions?

Two cities, then, have been created by two loves: the earthly by love of self extending even to contempt of God, and the heavenly by love of God extending to contempt of self.
Augustine

elements.text: We are all lovers of something. The question is: What is it that we love? At the most fundamental level, we have a clear choice: we can love God, or we can love ... something else.

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but they became futile in their thoughts and their senseless hearts were darkened. <sup>22</sup> Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools <sup>23</sup> and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for an image resembling mortal human beings or birds or four-footed animals or reptiles.

elements.question: What is wrong with worshipping something else instead of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says these people 'knew God' yet refused to glorify him or thank him, and the result wasn't neutral — their thoughts became 'futile' and their hearts 'darkened.' Then comes the trade: they 'exchanged the glory of the immortal God' for images of mortal humans, birds, animals, even reptiles. That's the wrongness of misplaced worship laid bare — it's a downgrade, swapping the one glorious, eternal God for something smaller and dying. And the claim to wisdom collapses into foolishness in the same breath. Worshipping the wrong thing isn't just misdirected devotion; it corrodes the mind and heart that do the worshipping.
elements.questionHint: Look at the word 'exchanged' — when you trade something immortal and glorious for an image of a mortal creature, what does that trade cost the person making it?

elements.text:
God himself should be our primary love. He should be the one we love with all our heart, mind, soul and strength. And because he is the Creator of all creation, part of loving him correctly will involve loving the rest of creation correctly too. Love of God is not an alternative to loving God’s creation; it’s the true basis for it.

This question of what, or who, we love is important in itself, and it is important because of the behaviour that it gives rise to. There is an order to sin and idolatry. Hearts that turn away from God become hardened; hardened hearts lead to darkened understandings which lead to indulging impurity. Corrupted affections lead to corrupted understandings which lead to impure behaviour.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> They are darkened in their understanding, being alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts.

elements.question: Where does giving your love, & heart, to the wrong thing end up?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This one verse traces a short, sobering chain: hardness of heart leads to ignorance, ignorance darkens understanding, and darkened understanding leaves a person 'alienated from the life of God.' So giving your heart to the wrong thing doesn't just disappoint you — it cuts you off, bit by bit, from the very life God offers. The word 'alienated' is key; it's not a gradual fading but an estrangement, like a relationship that's been broken. Wrong love hardens before it darkens, and it darkens before it isolates. That's where it ends up — not just wasted affection, but distance from God himself.
elements.questionHint: The verse starts with 'hardness of their hearts' as the root cause — what does hardness usually do to something over time, and where does that process end here?

elements.text: Even in wrongdoing, love motivates people - a disordered love, no doubt - but love nonetheless. People are not driven by their understandings (or misunderstandings!) alone. They are driven by what they love, informed by those (mis)understandings.

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it are the sources of life.

elements.question: Why is it important to guard where you set your heart?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Solomon calls the heart a wellspring: 'from it are the sources of life.' That single image explains the urgency of the command to guard it 'with all vigilance.' A spring doesn't just hold water for itself — everything downstream depends on what flows out of it. If the source is guarded and clean, life flows from it; if it's polluted or misdirected, everything that depends on it suffers too. Guarding your heart, then, isn't about repressing feeling — it's about protecting the origin point of your choices, desires, and actions, because whatever you allow to take root there eventually shows up everywhere else in your life.
elements.questionHint: The verse calls the heart the 'sources of life' — if a spring feeds everything downstream, what happens to the rest of the stream when the source itself is left unguarded?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> “Do not accumulate for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal. <sup>20</sup> But accumulate for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup> For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

elements.question: Why is it important to guard where you set your heart?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus contrasts two kinds of treasure: one earthly, vulnerable to 'moth and rust' and thieves, and one heavenly, immune to decay and theft. But the real punchline is verse 21: 'where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.' The heart doesn't lead the treasure — it follows it. So being careless about what you treasure isn't a side issue; whatever you invest in will inevitably capture your heart's attention and affection too. That's why guarding your heart means first being honest about what you're actually storing up. Choose treasure that can't rot or be stolen, and your heart will be anchored somewhere secure.
elements.questionHint: Verse 21 says your heart follows your treasure, not the other way around — so if you want to know where your heart actually is, what should you look at first?

elements.text: Love needs truth to endure - a ’love’, or a sentiment, unhinged from the truth will not last, since reality will at some point intrude to puncture its bubble. But bare facts don’t create strength and passion within us. Strength and passion are aroused by what we love, and will not easily be quenched:

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Set me like a cylinder seal over your heart, like a signet on your arm. For love is as strong as death, passion as unrelenting as Sheol. Its flames burst forth, it is a blazing flame. <sup>7</sup> Surging waters cannot quench love; floodwaters cannot overthrow it. If someone were to offer all his possessions to buy love, the offer would be utterly despised.

elements.question: Why is it important to be careful about what you set your love on?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage describes love in the most forceful terms possible — 'as strong as death,' with a passion 'as unrelenting as Sheol,' burning like 'a blazing flame' that no flood can quench and no fortune can buy. This isn't casual affection; it's a consuming, unstoppable force once it takes hold. That's exactly why where you set it matters so much. Love this powerful will reshape you, and if it's aimed at the wrong thing, that same unquenchable intensity becomes destructive rather than life-giving. Because love can't simply be bought, sold, or reversed on a whim, choosing its object carefully isn't optional — it's essential.
elements.questionHint: The passage says love can't be quenched by floods or purchased with 'all his possessions' — if love is that unstoppable and irreversible once given, why would its target matter so much?

elements.text:
Sometimes we treat people as if they were just brains rather than as ’lovers’. We (rightly) address people’s minds; we fail to address them as whole people. We work hard to know if people believe the right truths; we spend far less effort wooing people to love the right goods.

Sin is the proud attempt of the creature to reorder God and creation - to replace God with some part of creation. This helps us understand some of the more startling statements in the gospels.

elements.passageText: <sup>37</sup> “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.

elements.question: What does ordered and disordered love of parents look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states this bluntly: 'whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.' Disordered love of parents is loving them more than Christ — placing their approval, wishes, or claim on your life above his. Ordered love, by implication, still loves parents genuinely, but Christ occupies the position they cannot: the one whose claim comes first. This isn't Jesus dismissing family affection; it's Jesus refusing to be second to anyone, even the closest human relationships. The love itself isn't the problem — the ranking is. When any love, even a good one, outranks Christ, it has become disordered.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't say 'do not love father or mother' — he says not to love them 'more than me.' What does that specific wording tell you about what's actually wrong with disordered love?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Whoever insults his father or mother must be put to death.’

elements.question: What does ordered and disordered love of parents look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus quotes the command directly: 'God said, Honor your father and mother,' pairing it with the severe warning against insulting them. Notice the source — this is presented as God's own command, not merely a cultural nicety. That matters for understanding ordered love: honoring parents isn't in competition with loving God, it's part of obeying him. Disordered love would use devotion to God as an excuse to neglect or dishonor parents; ordered love recognizes that caring for family is itself something God has commanded and takes seriously, seen in how sharply he speaks about failing to do it.
elements.questionHint: The verse opens with 'For God said' — whose command is honoring your parents, according to this verse, and what does that do to the idea that loving God could excuse neglecting them?

elements.text: These verses seem to be at odds only if we do not see the importance of how love is ordered. The ’more’ (in Matthew 10:37) certainly refers to quantity of love (‘how much?’), but it also refers to a different kind or order of love. There is no ceiling on how much you should love a person as a person. But we must not love them as a god - not ever.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> Jesus answered, “The most important is: ‘Listen, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup> Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’

elements.question: What is the right way for our loves to be ordered?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus answers with the Shema and its command: love the Lord your God 'with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength,' calling it 'the most important.' The repeated word 'all' leaves no corner of a person exempt — feeling, will, intellect, and energy are all to be directed toward God. That's the right ordering: not a fragment of devotion alongside other loves, but total love for God placed at the very top, so that every other love in a person's life takes its proper shape and place underneath that first, all-encompassing commitment.
elements.questionHint: Count how many times 'all' appears in this command — what does that repetition suggest about how much of yourself is meant to be organized around loving God first?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> The person who does not love does not know God, because God is love.

elements.question: Why else does it makes sense that our lives are based on love?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John doesn't just say God loves — he says 'God is love.' That's an identity statement, not merely a description of behavior. Because love is who God is at his core, not just something he occasionally does, a life patterned after him will necessarily be a life of love. And John makes the connection sharp: 'the person who does not love does not know God.' Love becomes the evidence, even the test, of actually knowing him. If our lives are meant to reflect who God is, and God's very essence is love, then it makes complete sense that love would be the foundation everything else is built on.
elements.questionHint: The verse says 'God is love,' not 'God loves' — what's the difference between something being an action God takes and something being what God actually is?
