elements.text:
Case Study 4b - Michael & well-ordered love

Michael’s problem is not that he loves his job, nor that he wants to succeed. Work is a good gift from God, and we are called to work diligently. But his love for work is overshadowing his love for God and his family. Michael’s dedication to his job has distanced him from his family and his God. He is not consciously rebelling against God, but he is being drawn toward worldly success as his source of fulfilment.

Michael’s relationships are beginning to suffer. Rachel feels neglected, and his children are missing time with their dad. He may be telling himself he’s providing for his family, but the truth is that his presence and emotional support are more valuable to them than any material comforts his job may provide. Also, Michael’s spiritual life is starting to wither. His relationship with God is becoming secondary to his career ambitions. Michael may not realise it yet, but his disordered love for his work is pulling him away from the true source of joy and peace: God Himself. His misplaced love causes the weariness and frustration that Michael feels at home. His heart, designed to love God first and foremost, is being pulled in the wrong direction. No matter how much success he achieves, it will never satisfy the deeper longing in his soul for a relationship with God and a well-ordered life.

What does Michael need to do to realign his love? It is not (necessarily) about giving up his career or ambitions, but about restoring the proper order of love in his heart. (Although the further the ’disease’ is allowed to grow, the more drastic the ’treatment’ may need to be.) The greatest commandment is to love God with all our heart, soul, mind, and strength. Only when God is at the centre of our love can we rightly love everything else - including our families and our work.

For Michael, this may begin with repentance and prayer: acknowledging that success has drawn his heart away, and so he has neglected his primary love for God. He could also have an honest conversation with his boss about clearer work-life boundaries: perhaps limiting his hours to ensure he’s home in time for dinner, or turning off his phone during family time to be fully present. He should spend quality time with Rachel and his children. This could be as simple as family devotions, or planning regular family activities. He might also include Rachel in discussions about his career ambitions, ensuring that they are of the same mind on what is best for their family. This might mean reconsidering the promotion, if it will cause further damage, or finding ways to balance his professional growth with his family life.

Case Study 5 - Rachel (late 20s)

Rachel is a dedicated Christian. She has served in her local church since her teens. She leads a women’s Bible study, helps with the teens’ fellowship, volunteers in the church’s outreach programs. She’s known for being dependable, generous, and always willing to lend a helping hand. Rachel’s life is full, not only with church responsibilities but she also takes care of her widowed mother, who is not in good health. Rachel also has a full-time job as a high school teacher, which allows her to provide financially for herself and her mother.

For the past year or two, Rachel has felt her energy levels dropping. She is still committed to her faith in Jesus, and she regularly prays and reads her Bible, but she often feels worn out. She knows God is good and finds moments of encouragement in His presence, but the ongoing challenges of life are leaving her emotionally and physically drained. Some days she struggles to find joy even in the activities she used to love, like leading Bible studies and helping at church events. Rachel finds herself asking, ‘Why does life feel so hard, even when I’m trying to follow God faithfully?’ Her prayers for strength seem to be answered with more challenges.

Even with her weariness, Rachel still finds peace and contentment in God. She knows He is with her and there are still moments when she feels His presence encouraging her, but those moments are often fleeting. But the frustrations of her daily life - like difficult students at school, her mother’s health challenges, and conflicts in the church - are taking their toll. These problems pile up, and she sees no end to them. She wonders if she’s doing something wrong or if she just has to endure this difficult season indefinitely.

Flourishing is not measured by income, possessions, or status. It means becoming the person God had in mind when He created you.
John Ortberg

If you are not content with what you have, you would not be satisfied if it were doubled.
Charles Spurgeon

elements.text: People flourish when they are in a rightly ordered relationship with God, and with God’s creation - including other people, their environment, and their own self. We love God as God and we love people as people made in God’s image, as we love ourselves.

elements.passageText:
1 The Lord owns the earth and all it contains,
the world and all who live in it.

elements.question: How do we know that creation is good, and to be properly respected?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm grounds creation's value in ownership: 'The Lord owns the earth and all it contains, the world and all who live in it.' Nothing here belongs to us by ultimate right — it's his possession, from the ground beneath our feet to the people living on it. That ownership is exactly why creation deserves respect rather than careless use or contempt. We don't get to decide creation's worth on our own terms, because it was never ours to begin with; its value comes from belonging to the Lord, and treating it carelessly means mishandling something that isn't ours.
elements.questionHint: The verse says the Lord 'owns' the earth and everyone in it — if something belongs to someone else, what does that usually require of the way you treat it?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> for all things in heaven and on earth were created by him – all things, whether visible or invisible, whether thrones or dominions, whether principalities or powers – all things were created through him and for him.

elements.question: How do we know that creation is good, and to be properly respected?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up the scope deliberately — 'all things in heaven and on earth,' visible and invisible, even thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers — and says all of it was created 'by him,' 'through him,' and 'for him.' Creation's goodness isn't incidental or self-generated; it flows out of Christ as its source, was made by his agency, and exists for his purposes. Nothing falls outside that threefold claim. That's how we know creation deserves respect: it isn't random matter to be used however we like, but something intentionally brought into being by, through, and for Christ himself.
elements.questionHint: Notice the three prepositions used — 'by him,' 'through him,' 'for him' — what does using all three together say about how thoroughly creation belongs to Christ?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him,

elements.question: How do we know that love of created things can go wrong?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John draws a stark either/or: 'Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.' Notice this isn't a warning about moderation — it's exclusivity. Loving 'the world' as an ultimate object doesn't just crowd out love for the Father a little; it displaces it entirely, according to this verse. That's how we know love of created things can go wrong: not because things themselves are evil, but because when something created is loved in the place that belongs to the Father, both loves can't occupy that same space in a person.
elements.questionHint: The verse says if someone loves the world, the Father's love 'is not in him' — what does that wording suggest about whether these two loves can share the same top spot in a person's heart?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with the world means hostility toward God? So whoever decides to be the world’s friend makes himself God’s enemy.

elements.question: How do we know that love of created things can go wrong?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James doesn't soften this at all — he calls his readers 'adulterers' for choosing friendship with the world, a word that assumes a covenant relationship has been betrayed. He then spells out the logic plainly: friendship with the world 'means hostility toward God,' and choosing to be the world's friend actively 'makes himself God's enemy.' There's no neutral middle ground offered here. This shows love of created things goes wrong precisely when the world becomes a rival loyalty — not just a distraction, but something that positions a person in active opposition to God, the way infidelity positions someone against a spouse.
elements.questionHint: James uses the word 'adulterers' before he even explains what he means — what kind of relationship does that word assume has already been broken?

elements.text: Loving God’s creation as creation brings Him glory. The sin is when we love it the way we ought to love God alone.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> Jesus answered, “The most important is: ‘Listen, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one . <sup>30</sup> Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’

elements.question: Does loving God and loving people fit together? How/why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage only gives us half the picture on purpose — it names loving God with 'all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength' as 'the most important' commandment, full stop. It doesn't mention loving people here at all. But that's the point: this establishes the foundation everything else has to be built on. Loving God first, completely, isn't a rival to loving people — it's what makes any other love rightly ordered rather than idolatrous. Love for people fits underneath this greatest command, not beside it as a competitor.
elements.questionHint: This passage calls loving God 'the most important' commandment but doesn't mention neighbors at all here — what might that silence suggest about which love has to come first before the other one can be rightly ordered?

elements.text: Loving God involves loving his creation, including His image-bearers. There is no limit on loving others, if I love them as a person.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; I have come so that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.

elements.question: Is flourishing part of God’s plan for us? Why/why not?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus draws a sharp contrast between two agendas: 'the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy,' while he has come 'so that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.' The word 'abundantly' is doing real work here — Jesus isn't offering mere survival or bare existence, but overflow, fullness, more-than-enough life. That's a direct yes to flourishing being part of God's plan: it's explicitly named as the purpose of Jesus's coming, set against the destructive alternative. Flourishing isn't a distraction from following Jesus; according to this verse, it's precisely what he came to give.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't just say he came to give life — he says life 'abundantly.' What does that extra word add to what he's promising beyond mere survival?

elements.passageText: <sup>28</sup> Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. <sup>29</sup> Take my yoke on you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

elements.question: Is flourishing part of God’s plan for us? Why/why not?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus invites the 'weary and burdened' to come to him for rest, but the way he offers it is unexpected — he says 'take my yoke on you and learn from me,' not 'set down every burden.' A yoke is still work, still a load to carry. But it's carried alongside someone 'gentle and humble in heart,' and the promise is 'rest for your souls.' So flourishing, in this passage, isn't the absence of all effort or difficulty; it's found in whose yoke you're under. God's plan for flourishing runs through relationship with Jesus himself, not through escaping all labor.
elements.questionHint: Jesus offers rest but then immediately says 'take my yoke' — a yoke is a tool for work, not rest. Why might he combine those two ideas instead of just promising freedom from burdens?

elements.text: We were created to flourish: to enjoy God’s creation, to enjoy relationships with people, and to enjoy God. In this broken world, God is our rock and refuge: in Him is contentment, He cannot be taken from us, He will not let us down. Contentment and flourishing are not rivals. The opposite of contentment is discontentment, and the opposite of flourishing is withering. Look at this table.

Is the person flourishing?
Is the person content?YesNo
YesA: flourishing & contentB: withering, yet content
NoD: flourishing yet discontentedC: withering and discontented

Box A and Box C are straightforward. Box A is the ideal - how things would have been in an unfallen world, and how things can sometimes be even in our present world. Box C is also clear (but bad!). Box B shows God’s grace at work in our lives. Box D shows how sin distorts our lives, making us thankless, greedy or jealous, even in the face of blessing.

Box B is common. We can starve yet be content in Christ. But to flourish physically, we should eat healthily and enjoy it. Box B shows God’s grace at work in our life, despite something broken that prevents us from flourishing. It would be better if that brokenness could be fixed. We can be content in Christ when we lose a loved one and still cry our eyes out because part of us has been ripped away. It is a testimony to His goodness that we miss the one that he gave us.

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> Now we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who are asleep, so that you will not grieve like the rest who have no hope.

elements.question: As Christians, what is the wrong way to grieve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul frames it carefully: he doesn't want believers to be 'uninformed' about those who have died, precisely so that they won't 'grieve like the rest who have no hope.' The wrong way to grieve, according to this verse, isn't grieving itself — it's grieving as though there's nothing beyond death, the way people without any resurrection hope do. The problem is being 'uninformed,' missing the knowledge that reshapes grief. Christian grief is still real grief, but it's grief carried by people who know something others don't, which is why Paul is so intent on informing them rather than leaving them to sorrow blindly.
elements.questionHint: Paul says the goal is that they not grieve 'like the rest who have no hope' — what does that phrase imply is the actual problem: grief itself, or grief without something specific?

elements.text:
1 Thessalonians 4:13 is not a call to stop grieving, but a call to stop disordered grieving - grieving that knows no hope.

Which Box we end up in depends on whether our love of creation is ’ordered’ or ’disordered’. We are tempted to love created things in a disordered way, but that does not mean they should not be loved at all. The best things in life are both amazing and dangerous. When we love things in creation because we love our Creator, sorrow is appropriate as we grieve the loss of that created thing. ’Contentment’ and ’sorrow for loss’ are compatible. Box B is real, and since we live in a broken world, we will often find ourselves in it. Contentment is not a Stoic approach to life that ’rises above’ loving created things.

Seeking contentment in God alone, is not a rival to flourishing in relationships as God designed us. God is our Creator, so loving him involves loving his creation - but as creation, and not idolatrously.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> I have experienced times of need and times of abundance. In any and every circumstance I have learned the secret of contentment, whether I go satisfied or hungry, have plenty or nothing. <sup>13</sup> I am able to do all things through the one who strengthens me.

elements.question: Is it possible to be content, even when you are not flourishing? How?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul answers this from firsthand experience: he has known both 'times of need and times of abundance,' hunger and plenty, and in 'any and every circumstance' he has 'learned the secret of contentment.' That word 'learned' matters — contentment here isn't a natural disposition or a lucky temperament, it's something acquired, and acquired specifically 'through the one who strengthens me.' So yes, contentment is possible without flourishing, but not through willpower or positive thinking. It comes through a strength supplied from outside the circumstances themselves, which is why Paul can say the same thing whether he's satisfied or hungry.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls contentment something he 'learned,' and says he does 'all things through the one who strengthens me' — is the source of his contentment his circumstances, or something else entirely?

elements.text:
Case Study 5b - Rachel and Flourishing

Rachel’s weariness doesn’t mean she has failed in her faith or that God has abandoned her. Rather, it reflects the brokenness of this world, where even the most faithful servants experience hardship. Rachel’s contentment in God is a powerful testimony. Just because life is hard doesn’t mean God is not working. In fact, in these difficult moments, God’s sustaining grace often becomes most visible. Rachel can take heart knowing that even when she is weary, God is her refuge and strength. Even though she feels worn down, Rachel is living out the call to love others sacrificially. When she chooses to care for her mother instead of seeking her own comfort, she is reflecting the love of Christ. This is a form of flourishing that the world might not recognize, but it is the kind of flourishing that brings glory to God.

But Rachel also needs to consider how she can flourish physically and practically by addressing the pressures in her life, so she doesn’t wither contentedly. It may be appropriate for Rachel to re-evaluate the responsibilities she’s carrying. She has been pouring herself into caring for her mother, leading church ministries, and working full-time. She should consider whether it would be wise for her to change her level of commitment, either temporarily or permanently. She might speak with her church leaders about delegating some responsibilities to others. She could look at whether other family members could help sometimes with caring for her mother.

Perhaps Rachel could do more to look after her own health and rest. It’s easy for her to think that serving others means neglecting her own needs, but physical rest and self-care are essential for long-term flourishing. She could practise a regular time of Sabbath rest each week. She might benefit from simple things like regular exercise, and making time for things that bring her joy. Perhaps Rachel might also find more support from her community. She might invite members of her church to help with meals, running errands, or even spending time with her mother to give her some respite. This is not a sign of weakness but a way to allow others to serve her in love. Rachel might also need to establish clearer boundaries for her teaching work, to prevent burnout. She could create specific times when she is ’off duty’ from work-related tasks, like grading papers or answering emails. By protecting her evenings or weekends, she can safeguard time to rest and connect with her family.

It is great that Rachel has learned to be content. If she can also learn to flourish, she will be able to serve God faithfully over the long-term.

Case Study 6 - Ruth (mid-20s)

Ruth has been a Christian since primary school, growing up in a family that valued faith and attended church regularly. As an adult, she’s actively involved in her church’s worship team, often leading others in praise and worship. To those around her, Ruth seems to be thriving spiritually and musically - she has a beautiful voice, and people frequently compliment her for how she helps lead the congregation into meaningful worship. But what others don’t see is the deep sense of insecurity that Ruth carries with her.

Despite her outward confidence, she constantly feels like she’s not good enough, whether it’s in her job, her friendships, or even her relationship with God. Even though people praise her for her musical talents, she often downplays their compliments, feeling like she doesn’t really deserve them. She tells herself that if they knew the real her - the one who doubts her abilities and struggles to trust God fully - they wouldn’t be so impressed.

Ruth also tends to compare herself with others, especially when it comes to her appearance and achievements. Social media is a big trigger for her. As she scrolls through her feeds, she sees friends and acquaintances posting pictures of their accomplishments, holidays, and seemingly perfect relationships. She finds herself wishing she were prettier, more successful, or more talented. In these moments, her insecurity takes over, and she starts to believe that she’ll never measure up.

Yet as well, Ruth often feels overwhelmed by the desire to prove her worth to others, becoming eaten up by the need for validation. She’s caught between feeling unworthy and trying to find her worth through accomplishments and the approval of others.

Recently, during a prayer time, Ruth broke down and shared with a close friend how much she struggles with insecurity. She feels guilty for even thinking about her own worth and worries that loving herself might be selfish or prideful. Yet, she also feels empty and exhausted from constantly seeking approval and never feeling at peace with herself.

The most important thing is that we live for God and our neighbors; self-love is a distraction from this central calling.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Humility is not thinking less of yourself, it’s thinking of yourself less.
Tim Keller

Self-rejection is the greatest enemy of the spiritual life because it contradicts the sacred voice that calls us the ’Beloved.’
Henri Nouwen

elements.text: Should we love ourselves or not? Is self-love a form of selfishness to be avoided, or a form of wisdom to be embraced? The Bible’s approach can seem ambiguous.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, <sup>3</sup> unloving, irreconcilable, slanderers, without self-control, savage, opposed to what is good, <sup>4</sup> treacherous, reckless, conceited, loving pleasure rather than loving God. <sup>5</sup> They will maintain the outward appearance of religion but will have repudiated its power. So avoid people like these.

elements.question: What is self-love sometimes the opposite of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This list pairs 'lovers of themselves' right alongside 'lovers of money,' boastful, arrogant, and — tellingly — 'loving pleasure rather than loving God.' That last phrase names the real opposite directly: this kind of self-love displaces love of God, putting self and pleasure where God's place should be. It also produces the whole ugly list that follows — disobedience, ingratitude, lack of self-control — while keeping 'the outward appearance of religion' but denying its power. So self-love, in this sense, is the opposite of genuine godliness: it's a hollowed-out religion that has swapped love of God for love of self.
elements.questionHint: The list says people will be 'loving pleasure rather than loving God' — what does that 'rather than' tell you about which love this bad kind of self-love has pushed out?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> The one who acquires wisdom loves himself; the one who preserves understanding will prosper.

elements.question: Why is self-love sometimes a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This proverb links self-love to something surprising: wisdom. 'The one who acquires wisdom loves himself,' it says, and the one who 'preserves understanding will prosper.' Good self-love here isn't indulgence or vanity — it's wanting genuine wisdom and understanding for yourself, the kind that leads to real prosperity rather than fleeting pleasure. Seeking wisdom is actually an act of caring well for your own life, taking your own good seriously enough to pursue what will actually help you flourish. That's why self-love can be a good thing: when it's aimed at wisdom rather than ease, it's simply taking proper care of yourself.
elements.questionHint: The proverb connects self-love to 'acquires wisdom' rather than to comfort or pleasure — what does pursuing wisdom, instead of ease, reveal about what this kind of self-love is actually seeking?

elements.text: The Bible’s ambiguity is a signal to us that the issue of self-love is in itself ambiguous - or, perhaps better, it is complicated: there are ways in which self-love is good, and ways in which self-love is bad. From this angle, self-love is like anything else: there are ways it can be disordered, and ways it can be rightly-ordered.

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup> The second is: ‘ Love your neighbor as yourself .’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

elements.question: How does Jesus call us to love our neighbours?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states the second great commandment plainly: 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' and adds that no commandment is greater than these two together. The measuring stick he gives is telling — not an abstract ideal, but yourself. Whatever care, attention, and concern you already give your own needs and well-being becomes the standard for how you're to treat the person next to you. This assumes a person already has some baseline regard for their own life, and then calls them to extend that same quality of care outward. Loving neighbors, in Jesus's own words, is measured by the love you already know how to give yourself.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't invent a new standard for loving neighbors — he says 'as yourself.' What does using yourself as the measuring stick assume you're already doing for yourself?

elements.text: Loving our neighbours ’as ourselves’ assumes a rightly-ordered self-love and branches out from there to a rightly-ordered neighbour-love, where we recognise that our neighbours’ value and dignity are the same as our own, since we are all creatures created by God, and we should all be loved as such. A rightly-ordered Christian self-love will be a humble self-love. It will recognise the self as a fallen yet redeemed creature. It will value the self as a precious child of God, and it will root that value in the free gift of God (both through creation and redemption), not in some self-aggrandising, God-forgetting view of the self.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> For by the grace given to me I say to every one of you not to think more highly of yourself than you ought to think, but to think with sober discernment, as God has distributed to each of you a measure of faith.

elements.question: What does a selfish, disordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's warning is precise: don't 'think more highly of yourself than you ought to think,' but use 'sober discernment.' Disordered self-love looks like inflated self-assessment — rating yourself above the truth of who you are. Paul immediately grounds the corrective in something outside the self: the 'measure of faith' God has distributed to each person. That reframes everything — whatever gifts or standing you have were given, not self-generated, which should produce sober clarity rather than an inflated ego. Disordered self-love forgets that source and starts treating its own abilities as self-made achievements deserving of higher status than reality supports.
elements.questionHint: Paul says not to think of yourself more highly than you 'ought' — and then mentions faith God has 'distributed' to you. What does remembering it was given, not earned, do to an inflated self-view?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Instead of being motivated by selfish ambition or vanity, each of you should, in humility, be moved to treat one another as more important than yourself.

elements.question: What does a selfish, disordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul names the disordered pattern directly: being 'motivated by selfish ambition or vanity.' Both point to a self that's grasping for its own advancement or image, using others as a means to that end. The alternative he offers isn't just restraint but a full reversal — 'in humility,' treating others as 'more important than yourself.' That contrast makes the disordered version clear: selfish, vain self-love centers everything on your own advancement and appearance, calculating how situations serve you rather than others. It's a love of self that has crowded out any real regard for the people around you.
elements.questionHint: Paul pairs 'selfish ambition or vanity' against 'in humility' as the opposite motive — what do ambition and vanity have in common that humility specifically corrects?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> For where there is jealousy and selfishness, there is disorder and every evil practice.

elements.question: What does a selfish, disordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James is blunt about the fruit of this kind of self-focus: 'where there is jealousy and selfishness, there is disorder and every evil practice.' Notice how sweeping that is — not just some evil practices, but 'every' one, tracing back to jealousy and selfishness at the root. Disordered, selfish self-love isn't presented as a minor personal quirk; it's the soil that produces chaos and wrongdoing broadly. This shows that selfish self-love isn't a private matter that only affects the person who has it — James treats it as a source of disorder that spreads outward into every kind of evil practice.
elements.questionHint: James says jealousy and selfishness lead to 'disorder and every evil practice' — what does the word 'every' suggest about how far-reaching this kind of self-love's effects really are?

elements.text: Self-forgetfulness is sometimes presented as a cure for (wrongly ordered) self-love. This is a mistake. Both nature and psychology abhor a vacuum, so something will come in to fill it, and it probably will not be the right thing. Think of a sore limb - perhaps an infected hand - if you just ignore it, it will constantly demand more attention, and may even get worse. You will never be able to forget it! By healing it and giving it the attention it needs, it will be at peace, and not continually demand to be noticed. True self-forgetting comes not from ignoring the self, but from seeking its healing - and that comes through rightly-ordered, humble self-love.

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> I will give you thanks because your deeds are awesome and amazing. You knew me thoroughly;

elements.question: What does a humble, rightly-ordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist's response to being known and made isn't self-congratulation — it's thanks directed at God: 'I will give you thanks because your deeds are awesome and amazing.' The praise for being 'fearfully and wonderfully made' goes to the maker, not to the self admiring itself. Right alongside that sits a quiet comfort: 'You knew me thoroughly.' Humble, rightly-ordered self-love looks like this combination — genuine wonder at how you were made, paired with the security of being fully known, but with the gratitude aimed outward at God rather than inward at your own achievement or appearance.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist says 'I will give you thanks' about his own being — thanks to whom, and what does directing that gratitude outward rather than inward say about rightly-ordered self-regard?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? <sup>20</sup> For you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.

elements.question: What does a humble, rightly-ordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reframes the body entirely: it's 'the temple of the Holy Spirit,' and 'you are not your own' because 'you were bought at a price.' Rightly-ordered self-love, according to this passage, doesn't start from self-ownership at all — it starts from belonging to God. Because the body is sacred space, indwelt by the Spirit and purchased rather than self-possessed, caring for it becomes an act of honoring God rather than self-indulgence or self-neglect. The command that follows, 'glorify God with your body,' shows that healthy self-care and worship aren't separate categories here — they're the same act.
elements.questionHint: Paul says your body is 'the temple of the Holy Spirit' and that 'you are not your own' — if your body belongs to someone else, what does that change about the reason you'd take care of it?

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> For no one has ever hated his own body but he feeds it and takes care of it, just as Christ also does the church,

elements.question: What does a humble, rightly-ordered self-love look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul states something almost obvious to make his point: 'no one has ever hated his own body but he feeds it and takes care of it.' That ordinary, everyday nourishment and care is treated as normal and good — not vanity, just basic stewardship of what you've been given. He then raises the comparison: this is 'just as Christ also does the church.' Humble, rightly-ordered self-love looks like this unremarkable, practical care for your own body and needs, modeled on the same kind of attentive, nurturing love Christ shows the church — not indulgence, and not neglect either.
elements.questionHint: Paul compares feeding and caring for your own body to how 'Christ also does the church' — what kind of care does that comparison suggest is normal and good, rather than selfish?

elements.question: How do we learn to have a right attitude to ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord grounds identity in origin: 'My hand made them; that is how they came to be.' A right attitude toward yourself starts there — recognizing you were made, not self-created. But the verse pairs that with a specific posture that draws God's favor: he shows 'special favor to the humble and contrite, who respect what I have to say.' So the learning happens in two moves — remembering you were shaped by God's hand, and responding to him with humility and contrition rather than self-sufficiency. Right self-regard grows out of both truths held together: made by him, and humbly attentive to him.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> And God will exalt you in due time, if you humble yourselves under his mighty hand

elements.question: How do we learn to have a right attitude to ourselves?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter's instruction has a specific shape: 'humble yourselves under his mighty hand,' with the promise that God 'will exalt you in due time.' The right attitude toward yourself, according to this verse, involves a voluntary lowering — not self-loathing, but placing yourself under God's mighty hand rather than promoting or defending yourself. And notice where the timing sits: exaltation comes 'in due time,' which is God's timing, not yours to seize or rush. Learning a right attitude to yourself means trusting that if there's any lifting up to be done, it's God who does it, and he'll do it when he chooses.
elements.questionHint: Peter says God will exalt you 'in due time' if you first humble yourself — whose timing governs when any lifting up happens, and what does that ask you to do in the meantime?

elements.text:
Case Study 6b - Ruth indwelt by God’s truth

Ruth’s current struggle is a classic example of disordered self-love. Disordered self-love is not just about pride; it can also show up as anxiety and the need for constant validation. Ruth’s pattern of seeking approval from others will never satisfy her because our value is not based on human standards. True worth is rooted in God’s love for us and His creation of us as His beloved children.

To move forward, Ruth needs to see herself the way God sees her. That will help her embrace a rightly ordered, humble self-love.

Humble self-love knows that we are fallen, yet redeemed. Ruth needs to let this truth take up residence within her. She needs help in learning to shift her focus away from external comparisons and toward God’s truth about who she is. That way, she can rest in the knowledge that God already loves her fully and unconditionally, instead of seeking validation from others. Then she can escape the exhausting cycle of trying to prove her worth.

There are practical steps Ruth can take to help herself grow in this. She can take time to meditate on Scriptures that speak of her identity in Christ, so that these truths start to indwell and shape her. Replacing the lies of insecurity with God’s truth is a critical step in renewing her mind. She would be wise to limit her time on social media, since it sends her back into comparing herself to others. She may need to re-educate her inner voice, so that she speaks kindly and truthfully to herself, the way she would speak to others. She could also find help by sharing her struggles with trusted friends or mentors in her church community. They can offer her encouragement and remind her of God’s love when she’s feeling low.

As the truth of her worth in Christ begins to shape Ruth’s heart and mind, she will be better equipped to love others without seeking validation from them. Instead of relying on others to affirm her, she can serve in security and strength, knowing that her worth is already established in God. This frees her to love more selflessly, without the need to impress or compete.

Ruth will find true peace as she learns to rest in the knowledge that God delights in her. Self-rejection contradicts God’s own Word, that calls us ’Beloved.’ This is the foundation of a humble, rightly ordered self-love that leads to flourishing.

Case Study 7 - John (early-30s)

John came to faith at 27. He is married 8 years, has 2 kids and joined his church 6 years ago. Recently he started a new job with a probationary period, but 6 months in anxiety hits. He isn’t sleeping or eating well; he doesn’t know why he’s anxious.

John is heavily involved in church, leading Sunday School, serving as a deacon. He is keen to learn and has been to many church seminar days. He prays and reads his Bible often, ‘maybe not daily, but I certainly attempt to.’ He notices where help is needed, even when others don’t, and he will get stuff done; he is a hard worker. His marriage is strong, even compared with mature Christian couples.

John is a chronic nail biter. John remembers having stopped for nearly 4 months, but then he had a job interview he really wanted, and the stress started everything again. He hasn’t stopped since. John recalls a recent meeting with the eldership at church, where he was misunderstood, and seen as arrogant. It was a conversation about him becoming an elder. Before the meeting a friend who is an elder had suggested the outcome would be negative. John remembers going into the meeting feeling that there was no point in going ahead if the decision was already made.

John has a problem with porn. It was a struggle when he was first saved and it got better, although it still causes temptations, especially at more stressful times in life: deadlines in work, or maybe a bible study to prepare. He also talks about shouting at his children, finding parenting hard at times. He is constantly asking them to do the same things. His temper boils over a little too much for his liking.

For John school was difficult, he had a tough time with bullies and just wanting to fit in. He quickly went from girlfriend to girlfriend, rarely being outside of a relationship. At home John recalls a difficult relationship with his mother, they never got along. He had a good relationship with his uncle, his mother’s brother. As a teenager he went to work most summers with him. He remembers his uncle once breaking his wrist and being told to take it easy. This was during the school Easter holidays. John went to help him for 2 weeks, he was around 15 years old. He felt good because on the trip home his mother said, ‘I was told you worked really hard, well done.’ One other memory was when doing homework, John struggled with English and his mother got angry. He was around 12 years old, and clearly remembers his mother asking why he wasn’t as smart as the neighbour’s children. When asked about himself, John never talks about his good qualities. He focuses on the bad.

The proud man lives in fear of failure, and his anxiety comes from trying to hold up a false image. The humble man knows his value comes from God and rests in His assurance.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Pride is not thinking too much of yourself; it’s thinking of yourself too much. Anxiety follows when we are obsessed with our own significance.
Tim Keller

Pride is often a mask for our deepest anxieties, a way to cover our fragile ego.
Andrew Murray

elements.text: The original human Fall in Genesis 3 is often connected with the fundamental sin of pride. Adam and Eve listen to the serpent’s temptation to seek to be ’like God’ in a way that they shouldn’t be. They are already like God in every way that counts - they have been created in his image. elements.question: How does human pride echo Satan’s own pride
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah puts five boasts in the fallen king's own mouth: 'I will climb up to the sky... I will set up my throne... I will make myself like the Most High.' That's the anatomy of pride — not just wanting more, but wanting to occupy God's place, to rule from the highest point and answer to no one. Human pride runs the same script in miniature: we want our will, our judgment, our comfort enthroned above everything else, including God. And the passage shows exactly where that road ends — not enthronement but the pit, mocked by the very people who once feared 'the conqueror of the nations.'
elements.questionHint: Count how many times the fallen king says 'I will' before he's ever brought down — what does the pattern of those statements, more than any single one, tell you about what pride is reaching for?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> “Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, ‘This is what the sovereign Lord says: “‘Your heart is proud and you said, “I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods, in the heart of the seas” – yet you are a man and not a god, though you think you are godlike. <sup>3</sup> Look, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you. <sup>4</sup> By your wisdom and understanding you have gained wealth for yourself; you have amassed gold and silver in your treasuries. <sup>5</sup> By your great skill in trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart is proud because of your wealth. <sup>6</sup> “‘Therefore this is what the sovereign Lord says: Because you think you are godlike, <sup>7</sup> I am about to bring foreigners against you, the most terrifying of nations. They will draw their swords against the grandeur made by your wisdom, and they will defile your splendor. <sup>8</sup> They will bring you down to the pit, and you will die violently in the heart of the seas. <sup>9</sup> Will you still say, “I am a god,” before the one who kills you – though you are a man and not a god – when you are in the power of those who wound you? <sup>17</sup> Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom on account of your splendor. I threw you down to the ground; I placed you before kings, that they might see you.

elements.question: How does human pride echo Satan’s own pride
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse focuses on what's coming, not what was done: 'foreigners... the most terrifying of nations' will 'draw their swords against the grandeur made by your wisdom' and 'defile your splendor.' Notice the phrase 'made by your wisdom' — the pride here isn't abstract, it's pride in your own competence, in what you built and calculated. That's exactly how human pride often operates too: we don't usually claim to be gods outright, we just quietly credit our own wisdom for what we have and treat it as untouchable. This verse says otherwise — grandeur built on self-credited wisdom is precisely what gets defiled.
elements.questionHint: The verse says nations will draw swords against 'the grandeur made by your wisdom' — whose wisdom does it credit for that grandeur, and what does that tell you about where the pride was rooted?

elements.text: They over-reach themselves, and desire to be more than they are, and more than they should be, and more than they can be. This is self-aggrandisement on the largest scale, pride at its most fundamental.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> The Lord abhors every arrogant person; rest assured that they will not go unpunished.

elements.question: Why is pride dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse is blunt: 'The Lord abhors every arrogant person.' Not dislikes, not disapproves of — abhors, a word for something viscerally repulsive. That's a strong statement about how seriously God takes pride; it isn't a minor character flaw he overlooks in someone who's otherwise faithful. The second half adds the certainty of consequence: 'rest assured that they will not go unpunished.' Pride is dangerous, then, not because it's merely unattractive, but because it provokes God's active revulsion and guarantees a reckoning — there's no version of arrogance that quietly slips past him unnoticed or unaddressed.
elements.questionHint: The verse doesn't say God merely dislikes arrogance — it says he 'abhors' it. What does that stronger word suggest about how pride is different from an ordinary flaw?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> But he gives greater grace. Therefore it says, “ God opposes the proud , but he gives grace to the humble .”

elements.question: Why is pride dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James quotes an old proverb to make his point: 'God opposes the proud, but he gives grace to the humble.' Notice the verb — opposes. Pride doesn't just fail to earn God's favor, it actively puts you on the wrong side of him, like an adversary rather than a child he's helping. That's what makes it so dangerous: it forfeits the very thing you need most. The verse opens by saying 'he gives greater grace' — grace is available and abundant, but pride is the one posture guaranteed to be met with resistance instead of that grace.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God 'opposes' the proud rather than simply withholding blessing from them — what's the difference between God being unhelpful toward pride and God being actively against it?

elements.text: This fundamental sin of pride, and bias towards self-aggrandisement, is then inherited by the subsequent generations of humanity that follow from Genesis 4 onwards. We are born biased towards selfishness, Pride, and self-aggrandisement. However, this is not the full story. Precisely because our Pride is over-reaching, it does not correspond well to the situation in which we find ourselves.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

elements.question: Why is it wise to avoid pride?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: All we're given here is the first half of the proverb — 'Pride goes before destruction' — but even that fragment makes a claim worth sitting with: it's describing an order, a sequence. Pride isn't pictured as one danger among many that might befall a proud person; it's pictured as what precedes and leads to destruction, almost as its natural forerunner. Wisdom, in other words, isn't only warning that pride is wrong, but that it's a kind of signal — when you notice pride rising up in yourself, that's warning enough that a fall is already on its way.
elements.questionHint: The proverb says pride 'goes before' destruction rather than simply causing it — what does that word order suggest about pride functioning as a warning sign of what's coming?

elements.text: Humanity before the Fall is in a state of independent dependence - they are finite creatures dependent on an infinite God, but within that ultimate dependence they have great independence. They are to rule the cosmos as those who are the very image of God. This is a wide-ranging task, involving tremendous responsibility - and involves facing a massive, untamed creation - but they are equipped to undertake the task because their functional independence is rooted in fundamental dependence on God. Their freedom is a rooted freedom.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> If the Lord does not build a house, then those who build it work in vain. If the Lord does not guard a city, then the watchman stands guard in vain.

elements.question: How do we see that ’independent dependence’ at work in Scripture?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm doesn't tell the builder or the watchman to stop working — it says their work is 'in vain' without the Lord behind it. That's the paradox of independent dependence: real human effort (building, guarding) still happens, but its success was never actually in human hands to begin with. You can be diligent and skilled and still labor 'in vain' if the Lord isn't the one building or guarding through you. Scripture doesn't resolve this by asking us to do less, but by asking us to recognize whose effort was actually decisive all along.
elements.questionHint: The psalm says the builder's labor is 'in vain' without the Lord — does it tell the builder to stop building? What does that tension show you about how effort and dependence fit together?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> So then, my dear friends, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence but even more in my absence, continue working out your salvation with awe and reverence, <sup>13</sup> for the one bringing forth in you both the desire and the effort – for the sake of his good pleasure – is God.

elements.question: How do we see that ’independent dependence’ at work in Scripture?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul tells the Philippians to 'work out your salvation' — real, active effort is expected of them, 'not only in my presence but even more in my absence.' But he immediately grounds that command in verse 13: it is God 'bringing forth in you both the desire and the effort.' Even the wanting to obey, not just the doing, is credited to God's work in them. That's independent dependence exactly — genuine human striving sitting right alongside the truth that the will and the power behind that striving were God's gift all along.
elements.questionHint: Paul commands them to work, then immediately says God produces 'both the desire and the effort' in them — if God supplies even the wanting, what's left that's genuinely theirs to do?

elements.text: The Fall shatters this situation of rooted freedom. Post-Fall, we retain a great deal of freedom, but our freedom is now unrooted and adrift. We still face a massive, untamed creation, but now that creation is often hostile (sometimes lethally so), and we have cast ourselves adrift from the resources, guidance, and wisdom of an infinite God, and thrown ourselves onto our own finite resources instead.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> I will put a curse on people who trust in mere human beings, who depend on mere flesh and blood for their strength, and whose hearts have turned away from the Lord. <sup>6</sup> They will be like a shrub in the desert. They will not experience good things even when they happen. It will be as though they were growing in the desert, in a salt land where no one can live.

elements.question: Why does it make sense to respond to the world with anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage pronounces a curse on 'people who trust in mere human beings' and 'depend on mere flesh and blood for their strength' — and then pictures the result as a shrub stranded 'in a salt land where no one can live,' unable to notice good things even when they come. That image explains why anxiety is the natural response to relying on the world: human strength is 'mere flesh and blood,' inherently unstable ground to build a life on. If your security is rooted in something that can't sustain it, restlessness isn't an overreaction — it's an accurate read of how fragile that foundation really is.
elements.questionHint: The cursed person 'cannot experience good things even when they happen' — what does that detail suggest happens to your capacity for peace when your trust is planted in unreliable ground?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> But understand this, that in the last days difficult times will come. <sup>2</sup> For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, <sup>3</sup> unloving, irreconcilable, slanderers, without self-control, savage, opposed to what is good, <sup>4</sup> treacherous, reckless, conceited, loving pleasure rather than loving God. <sup>5</sup> They will maintain the outward appearance of religion but will have repudiated its power. So avoid people like these.

elements.question: Why does it make sense to respond to the world with anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul isn't describing distant strangers — he's describing 'difficult times' filled with people who are 'lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant... treacherous, reckless, conceited' while still keeping up 'the outward appearance of religion.' That combination is what makes anxiety a reasonable response to the world: the danger isn't only obvious hostility, it's that self-focused, untrustworthy character can hide behind a religious veneer, so you can't always tell who or what is safe. When Paul's own advice is simply 'avoid people like these,' he's acknowledging that this landscape really does call for caution, not naivety.
elements.questionHint: Paul says these people will 'maintain the outward appearance of religion' while having 'repudiated its power' — what does that gap between appearance and reality tell you about why the world can feel hard to navigate safely?

elements.text: We are often daunted in the face of the cosmos; our freedom falters and faints. Fallen humans are fundamentally anxious: we know that we do not have life in ourselves, and yet we have cast ourselves on our own resources, in the face of a world that overwhelms us.

elements.passageText: <sup>33</sup> I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble and suffering, but take courage – I have conquered the world.”

elements.question: What is the right response to this anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't promise the trouble will disappear — he says plainly, 'In the world you have trouble and suffering.' The peace he offers isn't the absence of hardship but something located 'in me': 'so that in me you may have peace.' The right response to anxiety, then, isn't denial that the world is genuinely hard, but courage rooted in a settled fact he states outright — 'I have conquered the world.' Trouble is real, but it isn't the last word; the last word belongs to the one who has already won, and peace comes from being found in him, not from circumstances changing.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says 'in me you may have peace' rather than 'in the world you will have no trouble' — where does he locate the source of peace, if not in circumstances improving?

elements.text:
Case Study 7b - Tell John a better story

Adult John needs to retell the story of his childhood. He needs to watch Jesus tell 12-year-old John a story about their heavenly Father who makes everyone special and unique, with different gifts, yet each is precious. Jesus says to young John:

Childhood is amazing for having fun and learning. As kids play and work, they find out what they are good at, what gifts God has given them. One day they will use those skills to bless others. Sometimes children struggle with this. They think everyone else’s gifts are better and get sad, or they think their gifts are the best and get proud. But gifts are as equally amazing as they are different. Enjoy your gifts and the gifts of everyone around you. The gifts are there for you to develop and enjoy and use to bring blessing to this broken world. Never be afraid to try stuff and fail, or to explore your gifts and make mistakes. You are exploring the person that God has made you, and He is delighted to see you try and fail and try again.

Sometimes when people are not feeling good about themselves, they say mean things to others. When someone says mean things like that to you, I want you to remember: it says more about how they are struggling than about you. I want to tell you a secret. Your mum is hurting. Someone has said mean things to her and she has said even meaner things to herself. She is feeling like a failure. She is hurting. And she is about to come over here and she wants to help you explore your gifts, but she can’t. And when she can’t, she is going to say something that she doesn’t believe and she doesn’t mean. And it will hurt. And it is something that no child should hear from their mother. And when she says it, I want you to see past her words and see her pain. This is not about you, it’s about her struggles. I want you to take the forgiveness I have given you and I want you to forgive her. She loves you. And even more, I love you. And you don’t need to be good at homework or anything else to get my love, you already have it, just look at the Cross - nothing could take my love from you. Now let’s sit here and try some more homework and together, we are going to explore your gifts and praise your father in heaven.

Those memories aren’t going away for adult John. They might be buried but what they need is the healing balm of the Gospel. Yes, John is guilty of disordered self-love, idolatry and pride. He needs to repent of seeking ultimate acceptance in the wrong places, but what he also needs is the Saviour. This is not a ’one time conversation.’ John will need to return to those childhood narratives many times, with Jesus by his side, telling a better, more truthful and gracious story.

Case Study 8 - Frank (mid-30s)

Frank is a Christian but struggles with identity, motivation and endurance in the Christian life. Frank was raised in a Christian home to caring parents. They lived in the countryside but were not farmers. His father was an outgoing people-person, who grew up in the town, and his mother an introverted countrywoman. He was the youngest child and grew up with little day to day interaction with anyone outside his family. He was taught not to be showy or proud but to quietly get on with life and to work hard. He trusted in Christ at an early age and was keen to please God at primary school which was very small. In academic selection (at aged 11) Frank’s siblings did not perform as well as hoped. Frank did better than expected. This was awkward for his parents to handle and confusing for Frank who was glad he did well but began to internalise that success was a source of embarrassment. Frank opted, with his parent’s encouragement, to go to the same high school as his siblings rather than the local grammar school as it was thought that he wouldn’t cope there. Throughout the rest of his school life he found that doing well in school came relatively easily but success was always something to be kept quiet or to be embarrassed about, at home and in school. In high school he fell between two groups of students: those raised in the farming community and those raised in the town (mostly from quite an aggressively loyalist area). Frank’s family lived in the countryside but were not farmers and so he felt he could not relate to either group.

As well as this, he was not maintaining a clear Christian witness and so maintained a lingering guilt. He had a feeling of not being comfortable either in his own skin or with those around him. He became highly afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing socially. Towards the end of high school the gospel began working on his heart; he began to be freed from the fear of man and started to follow Christ more closely. He began to serve in his church and on summer teams. After university and entering the working world he began with great hope for achievement and growth in his own life and in his work. The reality was, however, much more difficult and slow. There were many setbacks. He became afraid of failure and grew happy to just coast and please the people around him. Ambition and adventure in life became viewed as a suspicious source of pride or as too dangerous in case he fails. He struggles with self-discipline and establishing routines in his life. He recognises his lack of assertiveness over both his own life and his career and yet struggles to gain control. This in turn leads to further frustration and resignation.

Anxiety is often a byproduct of pride, where we think we must handle everything ourselves. In God’s hands, we find rest from both.
A.W. Tozer

Pride can mask itself as anxiety. We worry because we think we have to be in control. But when we humble ourselves, we learn to trust God with what we cannot manage.
Max Lucado

elements.question: What do you think of the above quotations? (Do you like them or not, and why?)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage

elements.text: Fallen humanity is biased towards two fundamental attitudes: pride (seeking to be like God in all the wrong ways), and anxiety (realising that we are ill-equipped to face a disordered universe in our own strength). We live with a sinful tension: we want to be gods and we realise we are not strong enough to be the gods we want to be(!)

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> “I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in me – and I in him – bears much fruit, because apart from me you can accomplish nothing.

elements.question: What should we realise instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus draws a direct line between remaining and fruit: 'The one who remains in me — and I in him — bears much fruit.' The realization he's pointing to isn't just that we need help sometimes, but something more total: 'apart from me you can accomplish nothing.' Not less, not little — nothing. Fruitfulness was never meant to come from self-generated effort branching off on its own; a branch doesn't produce by trying harder, it produces by staying attached to the vine. What we should realize instead of self-reliance is this ongoing, moment-by-moment connection as the actual source of anything worthwhile we do.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't say 'apart from me you can accomplish less' — he says 'nothing.' Why choose that absolute word instead of a milder one if he just wanted to encourage relying on him more?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But he said to me, “My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So then, I will boast most gladly about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may reside in me.

elements.question: What should we realise instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reports what God told him directly: 'My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' That's a strange kind of math — power isn't diminished by weakness, it's completed by it. What Paul realizes instead of pushing past his weakness or hiding it is to 'boast most gladly about my weaknesses,' precisely so that 'the power of Christ may reside in' him. The realization isn't resignation to limitation; it's recognizing that admitted weakness is the very place where Christ's power has room to show up and do its clearest work.
elements.questionHint: God says his power is 'made perfect in weakness' rather than in spite of it — what does 'made perfect' suggest about weakness's role, not just its presence?

elements.text: The right response to self, in the face of this combination of pride and anxiety, is to turn to God in faith and repentance, and to develop a well-ordered and humble self-love. Otherwise, we will develop one of two basic pathologies of self-love - everyday pride or everyday anxiety (or some variation of them, such as despair or apathy).

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> For by the grace given to me I say to every one of you not to think more highly of yourself than you ought to think, but to think with sober discernment, as God has distributed to each of you a measure of faith.

elements.question: What is the antidote to this wrong thinking?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's antidote to inflated self-opinion isn't self-hatred but recalibration: think 'with sober discernment,' seeing yourself accurately rather than either too highly or too low. And he grounds that sober view in a specific fact — whatever faith you have was something 'God has distributed to each of you,' a 'measure' assigned, not something you generated yourself. That reframes the whole comparison game: if your faith itself is a gift measured out by someone else, there's no basis for the kind of self-elevated thinking Paul warns against. Clear-eyed humility starts with remembering where what you have actually came from.
elements.questionHint: Paul says faith is a 'measure' God 'distributed' to you — if even your faith was assigned to you rather than earned, what happens to the case for thinking 'more highly' of yourself?

elements.text: We live in a broken world, as creatures estranged from our creator, and as guilty sinners who will one day give an account before our Judge. It is no surprise that we have a bent towards anxiety. The right response is to fix our eyes on God, in faith, repentance, and humility.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Instead of being motivated by selfish ambition or vanity, each of you should, in humility, be moved to treat one another as more important than yourself. <sup>4</sup> Each of you should be concerned not only about your own interests, but about the interests of others as well. <sup>5</sup> You should have the same attitude toward one another that Christ Jesus had, <sup>6</sup> who though he existed in the form of God did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, <sup>7</sup> but emptied himself by taking on the form of a slave, by looking like other men, and by sharing in human nature. <sup>8</sup> He humbled himself, by becoming obedient to the point of death – even death on a cross!

elements.question: What does humility look like, and involve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul defines humility by contrast and by action: instead of 'selfish ambition or vanity,' it means being 'moved to treat one another as more important than yourself.' It isn't only an internal attitude — it shows up as attention redirected outward: 'concerned not only about your own interests, but about the interests of others as well.' That second clause matters — Paul doesn't ask you to stop caring about your own interests, just to stop caring about only your own. And he anchors the whole instruction in a person: 'the same attitude... that Christ Jesus had,' making humility something modeled, not merely commanded.
elements.questionHint: Paul says to be concerned 'not only' about your own interests 'but about' others' too — does that mean dropping self-concern entirely, or expanding what you're concerned about?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> He has told you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord really wants from you: He wants you to promote justice, to be faithful, and to live obediently before your God.

elements.question: What does humility look like, and involve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The fragment we have doesn't yet spell out what the 'good' actually is — it only states that it has been told, plainly, to 'O man.' Even that much is worth noticing: God doesn't leave what's required for humility a mystery for us to guess at or philosophize toward. It 'has' already been told — past tense, settled, available. Whatever humility involves, according to this verse's own framing, isn't a hidden secret reserved for the spiritually elite; it's something already disclosed and expected to be known and acted on by ordinary people.
elements.questionHint: The verse says what is good 'has' already been told to you — what does that verb tense suggest about whether humility is a mystery you have to work out for yourself?

elements.text: If we do turn to Him, our anxiety is answered with reconciliation and peace, and our self-love is reset into humility. But as sinners, this is not our instinctive response. Instead we turn our gaze inwards, towards disordered self-love, and we trust in our self. We double-down on the mistake of pride and trust in the self that we want to be.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> But the one who boasts must boast in the Lord. <sup>18</sup> For it is not the person who commends himself who is approved, but the person the Lord commends.

elements.question: Where should we be looking instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a sharp contrast between two possible sources of approval: 'the person who commends himself' versus 'the person the Lord commends.' Only one of those, he says, is actually 'approved.' So where should we be looking instead of self-promotion or self-assessment? Toward the Lord's own verdict — 'the one who boasts must boast in the Lord.' That relocates the whole question of worth and achievement outside ourselves; it isn't our own résumé of accomplishments that settles anything, it's whether the Lord himself has commended it, which means we can stop performing for a verdict we were never qualified to render on ourselves.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts the one who commends himself with the one 'the Lord commends' — whose commendation does he say actually counts as being 'approved'?

elements.text: This ’idealised self’ that we trust in will then lead us towards one of two concrete outcomes: everyday pride or everyday anxiety. If we think we are (broadly) succeeding at becoming our idealised self in practice, then we will take pride in our self, and our achievements, and we will use that everyday pride to suppress our sense of anxiety. This comes at a cost. As well as the normal ugliness of a prideful life, there is the cost of keeping on proving that we are our ideal self.

elements.passageText:
4 The wicked man is so arrogant he always thinks,
“God won’t hold me accountable; he doesn’t care.”

elements.question: Why is pride so dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm gets specific about what makes the wicked man's arrogance so dangerous — not just that he thinks well of himself, but what he concludes about God: 'God won't hold me accountable; he doesn't care.' Pride here isn't just inflated self-regard, it's a functional atheism — arrogance that quietly edits God out of the picture as someone who notices or responds. That's what makes pride so dangerous: left unchecked, it doesn't just puff up the self, it talks itself out of any accountability at all, assuming indifference where there is actually a God who sees and cares.
elements.questionHint: The arrogant man's thought isn't 'there is no God' but 'he won't hold me accountable; he doesn't care' — what does pride do to your sense of being watched or answerable, even if you'd still say you believe in God?

elements.text: If we think we are (broadly) failing at becoming our idealised self in practice, then we will become increasingly anxious about our self, and our achievements - and that anxiety may lead us to despair. This also comes at a cost. As well as the normal stresses of an anxious life, we keep reminding ourselves of our failure to be our ideal self.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Do not be anxious about anything. Instead, in every situation, through prayer and petition with thanksgiving, tell your requests to God. <sup>7</sup> And the peace of God that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

elements.question: How does God call us to turn from anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul doesn't just forbid anxiety, he gives a replacement action: 'in every situation, through prayer and petition with thanksgiving, tell your requests to God.' The turn from anxiety isn't willpower or suppression — it's redirection, taking whatever was fueling the worry and handing it over in prayer, with thanksgiving mixed in even before the outcome is known. And the result isn't a guarantee that circumstances change, but that 'the peace of God that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and minds' — a peace that doesn't depend on things adding up logically, but stands guard regardless.
elements.questionHint: Paul pairs 'prayer and petition' with 'thanksgiving' before the situation is resolved — what does giving thanks in advance suggest about how this turn away from anxiety actually works?

elements.text: Everyday pride and anxiety are opposites, but they are also closely connected, as different expressions of the same disordered self-love. Anxiety is an upside-down version of pride. We condemn ourselves for not achieving all that we want, because we have too grand a view of our own powers. Anxiety and pride are two sides of the same coin - which is why some people flip between the two. Others, if anxiety cannot be sedated, turn to self-apathy, an attempt at self-numbing.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> And God will exalt you in due time, if you humble yourselves under his mighty hand <sup>7</sup> by casting all your cares on him because he cares for you.

elements.question: God calls us to a different life. What does that life look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter links two things that might seem opposite: humbling yourself 'under his mighty hand' and casting 'all your cares on him.' The different life God calls us to isn't self-sufficient toughness, and it isn't anxious self-management either — it's a kind of trusting surrender on both fronts, low before God's power yet unafraid to hand him every worry. And there's a promise attached to the humility: 'God will exalt you in due time.' The casting of cares is grounded in a stated reason, not just an instruction: 'because he cares for you' — the trust makes sense because the one receiving the cares is already invested in you.
elements.questionHint: Peter gives a reason for casting your cares on God — 'because he cares for you' — how does that reason change casting cares from a technique into something more like trust in a person?
