elements.text:
Case Study 8b - Tell Frank a better story

Frank needs to retell that story of his childhood, to have Jesus take 11 year old Frank by the hand and celebrate his academic achievement, to explain to him that his parents are trying to protect him, he needs Jesus to explain to 11 year old Frank that God has given him a wonderful gift to be used and celebrated and that God is going to equip little Frank with skills that are going to be a blessing in this broken world, that God’s grace in saving him from sin is the same amazing grace that sends him out in the name of Christ, confident that he is going to be used by God (Ephesians 2:8-10).

30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus take 11 year old Frank by the hand and explain what happened. Assuming that Frank’s parents were trying to teach humility (rather than trying to suppress his gifts), 30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus talk to 11 year old Frank, to assure him that his gifts are special and that he has been given them to be used and make a difference in this world, he needs to watch as Jesus encourages 11 year old Frank to forgive his father, maybe not for wilfully trying to damage Frank but for missing the impact of his words.

30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus as he talks to 11 year old Frank, as Jesus asks him about all he learnt in School and watch how Jesus smiles from ear to ear, celebrating the heavenly Father that gives every good gift (James 1), he needs to watch as Jesus draws Frank close to himself and as they sit in the boat together, older Frank needs to watch as Jesus embraces little Frank, as he silently unties the rope and gently pushes the boat away from the harbour, and says to him, ‘let’s do this together’.

As Frank’s affections are reordered, as he stops fearing that godly ambition equals pride and family rejection, as Jesus’ words start to bring healing to his self-understanding, then he may have the freedom to develop godly ambition and drive.

Case Study 9 - Edward & Mary (late-40s)

Edward has just initiated and completed a divorce. He had been married to Mary for 15 years and they have 2 children together. Edward had lost interest in sex with Mary and when they went through the divorce, he told Mary that he had known for a long time that he didn’t feel like he loved her. He said he had always struggled with it and didn’t think he ever did really love her. He had tried to convince himself that he did, that’s why he married her, but he had been living a lie in their marriage.

A few months after the divorce, Edward calls Mary to say he has made a mistake. His life is empty, he needs her back.

  • Edward loves the healthy lifestyle. He has a strict exercise routine, only eats healthy food, treats his body like a temple. Sometimes obsessively so.
  • He only had one long term girlfriend before he married Mary. He broke up with her for the same reason. He didn’t feel like he really loved her.
  • He absolutely loves his job; he is a lawyer and he is passionate about what he does. He has been very successful and has a reputation for getting what he wants, even if he has to be ruthless with people to get it.
  • Apart from their wedding day, Mary has no memory of them spending any time with Edward’s parents. Occasionally Edward talks about his Dad and has fond memories. He never talks about his Mum. If Mary ever pushed for information, Edward would just say that she was a hard woman and they have drifted apart.
  • Edward’s mother was an insecure, angry lady. Edward craved to be hugged and cared for. At age 9 Edward came home after being seriously bullied and his mother showed no compassion and told him that he probably deserved it.

Take away all love and hatred, all hope and fear, all anger, zeal, and affectionate desire, and the world would be, in a great measure, motionless and dead.
Jonathan Edwards

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> Counsel in a person’s heart is like deep water, but an understanding person draws it out.

elements.question: Why is it hard to understand ourselves and others?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb compares what's inside a person to 'deep water' — not hidden exactly, but not visible on the surface either, requiring real effort to reach. That's why it's hard to understand ourselves and others: our actual motives, the 'counsel' driving our choices, sit below what's easily observed, including to ourselves. The proverb doesn't say this depth is unreachable, though — it says 'an understanding person draws it out,' which takes patience and skill, like drawing water from a well rather than glancing at a puddle. Self-knowledge and knowing others both require that same slow, deliberate work.
elements.questionHint: The proverb compares a person's inner counsel to 'deep water' rather than a puddle — what kind of effort does drawing water up from a well require that glancing at a surface doesn't?

elements.text: Four clues can help us understand the loves at the centre of our hearts: desire, joy, fear, and sorrow. When we love something, we pursue it - we desire the joy of being satisfied by it. When we love something, we protect it - we fear the sorrow of losing it.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For those who live according to the flesh have their outlook shaped by the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit have their outlook shaped by the things of the Spirit.

elements.question: How do our desires and fears help reveal our hearts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws the line at what shapes a person's 'outlook' — those who 'live according to the flesh have their outlook shaped by the things of the flesh,' while those who live by the Spirit are shaped by the things of the Spirit. That's exactly how desires and fears expose the heart: whatever you set your mind on, whatever you're drawn toward or anxious about, is already revealing which direction is forming you. Desires and fears aren't just passing feelings — according to Paul, they're evidence of which 'things' currently occupy and shape your inner orientation, flesh or Spirit.
elements.questionHint: Paul says people's 'outlook' is 'shaped by' whatever they set their mind on — what does that suggest your desires and fears are actually doing to you, beyond just reflecting how you already feel?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom you should fear: Fear the one who, after the killing, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>7</sup> In fact, even the hairs on your head are all numbered. Do not be afraid; you are more valuable than many sparrows. <sup>32</sup> “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is well pleased to give you the kingdom.

elements.question: How do our desires and fears help reveal our hearts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus redirects fear rather than eliminating it — 'do not be afraid of those who kill the body,' but 'fear him' who has authority beyond death. That contrast exposes the heart: what you're actually afraid of shows what you think has ultimate power over you. Then Jesus pivots from fear to worth and desire: 'even the hairs on your head are all numbered... you are more valuable than many sparrows,' and 'your Father is well pleased to give you the kingdom.' Rightly placed fear and rightly placed desire both trace back to the same reality — whether you know yourself as cared for by this Father or not.
elements.questionHint: Jesus moves from telling them whom to fear straight into telling them how valued and cared for they are — why put those two things next to each other?

elements.text: Desires are not bad; they are good, and it would be bad to lose them. We can desire wrong things, just like we can do wrong things - but the solution is not to desire nothing - that would make us less human, and more like a rock. Desires are part of how God created us.

elements.passageText:
4 May he grant your heart’s desire;
may he bring all your plans to pass!

elements.question: How do we know that having desires is a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is a blessing, not a warning — 'May he grant your heart's desire; may he bring all your plans to pass!' Someone praying this over another person clearly doesn't treat desire itself as suspect or dangerous; it's something worth asking God to fulfill. That tells us desires can be good: they're not automatically selfish or dangerous impulses to suppress, but can be exactly what a good God delights to grant. The verse assumes desire and plans are a normal, even hoped-for, part of a flourishing life under his blessing.
elements.questionHint: The verse is phrased as a prayer of blessing over someone's desires, not a warning against them — what does praying for someone's 'heart's desire' to be granted assume about desire itself?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Praise the Lord , O my soul! Do not forget all his kind deeds! <sup>3</sup> He is the one who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases, <sup>4</sup> who delivers your life from the Pit, who crowns you with his loyal love and compassion, <sup>5</sup> who satisfies your life with good things, so your youth is renewed like an eagle’s.

elements.question: How do we know that having desires is a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist lists desire after desire that God has already met — forgiveness for sin, healing for disease, deliverance from the Pit, being 'crowned' with love and compassion, and having his life 'satisfied... with good things.' None of these are treated as improper longings; they're 'kind deeds' worth actively remembering, worth telling your own soul not to forget. That's the evidence that desire is good: God is pictured here as someone who delights to satisfy real needs and longings, right down to renewing youth 'like an eagle's' — abundant, generous fulfillment, not stingy suspicion of wanting things.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist calls God's answers to these longings 'kind deeds' worth actively remembering — what does calling them 'kind' rather than merely 'necessary' suggest about how God views satisfying desire?

elements.text: Fears and desires can often be connected to sin within us. If we are driven by pride and/or anxiety, then our desires and fears will be connected to that pride or anxiety. Thus, if someone’s desires are threatened, and/or their fears are triggered, pride or anxiety may colour the way they respond. This is not because desires and fears are wrong in principle. Desires and fears are good to have! We seek what we love, we long for it and pursue it. Desire begins the search. The stronger the love, the more intense the desire, the more relentless the search, the more satisfying the embrace. We desire what we love, and we feel joy as we move towards the objects of our desire.

elements.passageText:
6 The righteousness of the upright will deliver them,
but the faithless will be captured by their own desires. 23 What the righteous desire leads only to good,
but what the wicked hope for leads to wrath.

elements.question: Why can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: These proverbs put desire on a spectrum rather than condemning it outright: 'what the righteous desire leads only to good,' while 'the faithless will be captured by their own desires' and 'what the wicked hope for leads to wrath.' The word 'captured' is telling — desire doesn't just misfire occasionally for the faithless, it takes them prisoner, becomes something that controls rather than serves them. So the problem isn't desire itself, since righteous desire leads to good; the problem is what's being desired and by whom, since the same capacity can either deliver good or become a trap that owns you.
elements.questionHint: The faithless aren't just disappointed by their desires, they're 'captured' by them — what does that word suggest happens when a desire stops being something you have and starts being something that has you?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> But I say, live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh. <sup>17</sup> For the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh, for these are in opposition to each other, so that you cannot do what you want. <sup>24</sup> Now those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

elements.question: Why can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes an actual civil war inside a person: 'the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh... so that you cannot do what you want.' That last phrase is the real problem with desire — it's not unified or trustworthy, since even your own wanting is internally divided against itself. That's why desires can be a problem: left to themselves, they pull in contrary directions and leave you unable to simply do what you want. Paul's answer isn't better willpower but a decisive act — those who belong to Christ 'have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.'
elements.questionHint: Paul says the flesh and Spirit's opposing desires mean 'you cannot do what you want' — what does it say about desire that even doing 'what you want' becomes impossible?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> Dear friends, I urge you as foreigners and exiles to keep away from fleshly desires that do battle against the soul,

elements.question: Why can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter's language is military: fleshly desires 'do battle against the soul.' That's a strong claim — these desires aren't neutral preferences competing politely for attention, they're actively fighting to win against the deeper part of you. He also calls believers 'foreigners and exiles,' which matters here: indulging desires that belong to our old home means fighting for a home we've already left. That's why desires can be a problem — not because wanting things is inherently wrong, but because some desires are actively working against the soul's good, not just distracting from it.
elements.questionHint: Peter says these desires 'do battle against the soul' — what does military language like 'battle' suggest about desire's danger, compared to just calling it a 'distraction'?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry.

elements.question: How should we deal with wrong desires?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's instruction is deliberately severe: 'put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth.' Not manage, not moderate, not gradually redirect — put to death, language for a decisive, final act rather than ongoing negotiation. The list he gives ends with a striking equation: 'greed which is idolatry.' That's the key to dealing with wrong desire — it names what's really happening underneath it. A wrongly directed desire isn't just excessive wanting, it's worship misplaced onto something other than God, and worship misplaced that seriously can't just be trimmed back; it has to be killed.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls greed 'idolatry' rather than just excess — what does naming a wrong desire as worship, rather than simply as too much wanting, suggest about how seriously it needs to be dealt with?

elements.text: Fear and sorrow are mirror images of desire and joy. We fear the loss of the things that we love, and we experience sorrow if and when our fears are realised - if and when that loss occurs.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> And if you address as Father the one who impartially judges according to each one’s work, live out the time of your temporary residence here in reverence.

elements.question: When is fear good, and when is it bad?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter connects fear to a specific identity: we address God 'as Father,' yet this Father also 'impartially judges according to each one's work.' That combination shapes what good fear looks like — not a Father who abandons discipline, and not a judge who is anything but fair, but both held together, producing 'reverence' rather than either presumption or terror. He adds that this reverence is meant to mark 'the time of your temporary residence here,' as if fear rightly understood is part of living as someone who doesn't fully belong to this present place yet answers to the one who does the judging.
elements.questionHint: Peter calls God both 'Father' and one who 'impartially judges' in the same sentence — how does holding those two together shape 'reverence' differently than fearing a judge alone would?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> For everyone who does evil deeds hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds will not be exposed.

elements.question: When is fear good, and when is it bad?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus explains the mechanics of a bad fear: those doing evil 'hate the light and do not come to the light, so that their deeds will not be exposed.' That's fear functioning as self-protection — not reverence toward someone greater, but avoidance driven by not wanting to be seen accurately. This is a fear that keeps you away from the very thing that could actually help you, because what you're really afraid of is exposure, not wrongdoing itself. Bad fear, by this measure, is the kind that steers you toward hiding rather than toward the one who sees clearly.
elements.questionHint: The verse says people avoid the light so their deeds 'will not be exposed' — what is that fear actually protecting, and what is it protecting it from?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Even when I must walk through the darkest valley, I fear no danger, for you are with me; your rod and your staff reassure me.

elements.question: How should we deal with wrong fears?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The line we have names the danger honestly — 'the darkest valley' — without minimizing or explaining it away; there's no pretending the valley isn't dark or that walking through it is easy. That honesty is itself part of how Scripture deals with wrong fears: it doesn't ask you to deny that hard, frightening seasons exist. What the verse offers as an answer to that fear is signaled by its own phrasing — 'even when' sets up a contrast, implying that whatever follows is meant to hold true precisely within the darkest circumstances, not only once you're safely past them.
elements.questionHint: The phrase 'even when' sets up a contrast with something that follows — what kind of statement would need to come next to make walking through 'the darkest valley' something other than simply fearful?

elements.passageText:
7 Fearing the Lord is the beginning of moral knowledge,
but fools despise wisdom and instruction. 4 Then you will take delight in the Lord,
and he will answer your prayers.

elements.question: Who should we fear, and desire?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: These two half-verses point the same direction from opposite angles: fear and desire. 'Fearing the Lord is the beginning of moral knowledge' — real wisdom starts by rightly fearing him, while 'fools despise wisdom and instruction' by skipping that step. Then Psalm 37 adds the desire side: 'take delight in the Lord, and he will answer your prayers.' So the same God is meant to be both feared and delighted in — not two contradictory postures, but two sides of taking him seriously as who he actually is. Whoever or whatever fills those two roles for you, fear and desire, functions as your real god.
elements.questionHint: One verse says to fear the Lord and the other says to delight in the Lord — how can the same relationship hold both fear and delight together instead of one canceling out the other?

elements.text:
Case Study 9b - Edward’s fears and desires

Despite what he said at the time, it seems Edward didn’t divorce Mary because of a lack of affection or desire for her, but because of his love for control, and his fear of emotional intimacy. Those desires and fears overshadowed his love for her (and his fear of loneliness). He believed that distancing himself from the relationship would solve his discomfort.

But once the divorce was final, Edward’s other fears - of isolation and loneliness - began to become dominant again, as did his love for Mary and their children. Without the relationship, his life felt empty, and he realised that Mary’s presence brought him a sense of stability and joy that he hadn’t fully appreciated. Edward’s call to Mary, months after the divorce, reveals a shift in the cycle of his desires. His need for control and distance is no longer in the driving seat, and he is becoming more and more conscious of his desire to reconcile and find meaning in the relationship he had discarded. He realises that his life feels incomplete without Mary and their children, and that the pursuit of his personal ambitions has left him unfulfilled.

However, unless Edward changes on a deeper level, he is likely to repeat the same cycle. Even if Mary took him back - or even if he eventually entered a relationship with someone else - unless he addresses the deep things going on in his heart, he will in time cycle back to his desire for control and fear of intimacy.

To move forward, Edward must confront the deep fears and desires that rule his life. He must learn to turn from them towards God as his foundation. His misshapen fears and desires flow from his disordered loves. He needs to understand that his desires can only be met in God, and his fears only overcome in God. Without correcting those foundations he will find it difficult to desire healthy relationships with others, and embrace vulnerability, rather than fear it. This will require repentance and a new understanding of how love works - not as a tool for control, but as a foundation of selfless connection, allowing his desires to be reshaped by God’s love and truth.

Case Study 10 - Glen and Jennifer (mid-30s)

Glen and Jennifer go to church. Jennifer comes across as a private person and doesn’t connect with many people at church. They don’t support the church financially and Jennifer hates always being asked to serve.

Glen’s Perspective: We’ve been married 5 years. I was attracted to Jennifer as she was so strong and driven and such a good mother to her son Bobby (he is 16). She says she doesn’t want any more children and won’t engage with the fact that I really do. It’s like she is always looking out for herself. She keeps her own savings account and even if things are tight, she’ll dip into it to go to a beauty salon, but I can’t touch it to help cover car repairs. She worked her way up to being the store manager at the local supermarket, but the rest of staff hate working for her. She micromanages them; everything has to be done her way. I know how they feel. Jennifer gets very jealous of me spending time with the lads. I used to go out with them on Fridays, but it caused arguments each time, so I stopped. Her son Bobby has started dating a lovely girl. Jennifer is nice to the girl’s face, but when she’s gone, Jennifer picks holes in her. I’ve told her that she can be selfish sometimes. She says she knows; her own mother used to say the same. She says she doesn’t want to be selfish and will try harder. I’ve told her that micromanaging people drives them away - she knew I was talking about more than the supermarket staff.

Jennifer’s Background: Her parents split when Jennifer was 11 years old, she was the oldest child of 4 siblings. Her father said he loved her very much and would still see her every weekend - but soon he just dissolved out of her life. Jennifer started secondary school aged 12. Her best friend from primary school was in her class. When her friend started to make new friends, Jennifer got so angry with her. It wasn’t long before they weren’t speaking. They never made up.

Her brothers and sisters were always quite ’care-free’, but Jennifer was an anxious teenager. She didn’t sleep well at night, and seemed on edge if her mum or siblings were gone for a long time. Her mother started to date another man, Jennifer made it clear that she didn’t want this man in the home even though she couldn’t point to anything wrong with him. Her mum told her off for not caring about anyone’s happiness but her own. As her siblings got older, Jennifer didn’t like sharing her stuff with them. Her mum and siblings said she was getting more and more selfish. Her mum would insist she shared, or take the stuff off her when she refused.

She worked hard at school and wanted a successful career. At university she started dating. Her boyfriend was charming, got her pregnant, and then left her. She raised her son Bobby alone and started working part time in the local supermarket. She taught him to ’work hard’ and ’tell the truth’. She often told him that people who lie are worthless. At 30 she married Glen. He’s a good husband and step-father.

Never be afraid to trust an unknown future to a known God.
Corrie ten Boom

elements.text:
This study, and the next two, focus on three fears that repeatedly arise in our situations as fallen, finite, and free creatures of God: Am I safe? Am I valuable? Do I belong? We will look at them in turn.

We feel safe with others when three factors come together: (i) sacrifice - the other person cares for me and will put me first; (ii) competence - they are strong and skilled enough to protect me; and (iii) connection - they understand me and know what I need.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> For while we were still helpless, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. <sup>7</sup> (For rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might possibly dare to die.)    <sup>8</sup> But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is careful about the timing here: Christ died for us 'while we were still helpless' and 'while we were still sinners' — not after we'd cleaned ourselves up or proven ourselves worth saving. He even contrasts this with normal human loyalty, where someone might risk dying for a truly good person, but rarely for anyone else. God's love didn't wait for us to become good. That's why our safety with God isn't fragile or conditional on our performance — it was demonstrated and settled at the point we least deserved it, which means it can't be undone by our ongoing weakness either.
elements.questionHint: Look at the timing words 'while we were still helpless' and 'while we were still sinners' — what does it mean that Christ's death happened before any improvement on our part, not after?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> God is our strong refuge; he is truly our helper in times of trouble. <sup>2</sup> For this reason we do not fear when the earth shakes, and the mountains tumble into the depths of the sea, <sup>3</sup> when its waves crash and foam, and the mountains shake before the surging sea.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm doesn't promise that nothing frightening will happen — it pictures the worst-case scenario directly: the earth shaking, mountains tumbling into the sea, waves crashing and foaming. Yet the response is 'we do not fear.' That's because safety here isn't defined by calm circumstances but by who God is in the middle of the chaos — 'our strong refuge,' 'our helper in times of trouble.' The confidence isn't that trouble won't come, but that even if the most stable things in creation gave way, God himself wouldn't. Our safety is anchored in him, not in the absence of shaking.
elements.questionHint: Notice the psalm imagines the most extreme instability possible — mountains falling into the sea — and still says 'we do not fear.' What does that say about where the safety actually comes from?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. <sup>16</sup> Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The reason we can approach God 'confidently' rather than nervously is spelled out plainly: our high priest isn't someone incapable of sympathizing with us, but one who was 'tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin.' He knows weakness from the inside, not from a safe theoretical distance. That's what lets us come to 'the throne of grace' expecting mercy and help rather than rejection. If Jesus had never faced real temptation and pressure, we might reasonably fear he'd have no patience for our struggles. Because he does understand, we can come honestly, without needing to hide our weakness first.
elements.questionHint: The passage says Jesus was 'tempted in every way just as we are' — how does knowing the one you're approaching has actually faced what you're facing change whether you come to him confidently or fearfully?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> “ Look! The virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call him Emmanuel,” which means “ God with us .”

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The whole weight of this verse sits in the name itself. Matthew doesn't just report that a son will be born — he stops to translate the name for us: Emmanuel means 'God with us.' That's the safety being promised here. It isn't that God sends help from a distance or issues instructions from far away; he comes to be present, right in the middle of human life, sharing the same space and conditions we live in. A God who is with us, in person, is a fundamentally different kind of safety than a God who merely watches over us from somewhere else.
elements.questionHint: The verse pauses to translate the name 'Emmanuel' for us — what does that translation itself say about where God chooses to be in relation to us?

The opposite is also true. I will feel unsafe to entrust myself to a given person if they are selfish (lack of sacrifice), or if they are weak (lack of competence), or if they don’t ’get’ me (lack of connection - a significant issue for teenagers). elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> There was a famine in the land, so Abram went down to Egypt to stay for a while because the famine was severe. <sup>11</sup> As he approached Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman. <sup>12</sup> When the Egyptians see you they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me but will keep you alive. <sup>13</sup> So tell them you are my sister so that it may go well for me because of you and my life will be spared on account of you.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in these passages?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Abram's fear runs the calculation out loud: if the Egyptians know Sarai is his wife, 'they will kill me but will keep you alive.' To protect his own life, he asks her to say she's his sister — a half-truth that leaves her exposed to being taken into someone else's household while he stays safe. Fear over his own safety makes him willing to sacrifice hers. It's a striking picture of how self-protective fear doesn't just make us cautious — it can make us willing to use the people closest to us as a shield, treating their safety as expendable for our own.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Abram asks Sarai to do and who benefits from the lie — whose safety is he actually protecting, and at whose expense?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup> But the men who had gone up with him said, “We are not able to go up against these people, because they are stronger than we are!” <sup>32</sup> Then they presented the Israelites with a discouraging report of the land they had investigated, saying, “The land that we passed through to investigate is a land that devours its inhabitants. All the people we saw there are of great stature. <sup>33</sup> We even saw the Nephilim there (the descendants of Anak came from the Nephilim), and we seemed liked grasshoppers both to ourselves and to them.” <sup>1</sup> Then all the community raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. <sup>2</sup> And all the Israelites murmured against Moses and Aaron, and the whole congregation said to them, “If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or if only we had perished in this wilderness! <sup>3</sup> Why has the Lord brought us into this land only to be killed by the sword, that our wives and our children should become plunder? Wouldn’t it be better for us to return to Egypt?” <sup>4</sup> So they said to one another, “Let’s appoint a leader and return to Egypt.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in these passages?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The spies don't lie about the facts — there really were strong people and fortified cities — but their fear reframes everything: 'we seemed like grasshoppers both to ourselves and to them.' That self-image, born of fear, spreads instantly to the whole community, who weep all night and start talking about appointing a new leader to take them back to Egypt. Fear over safety doesn't stay private; it becomes contagious and starts rewriting the story of who they are. Ten men's fear convinces an entire nation that slavery in Egypt would be safer than trusting God for the promise he'd already begun keeping.
elements.questionHint: Notice the phrase 'we seemed like grasshoppers both to ourselves and to them' — how did their own self-image, shaped by fear, end up driving the whole nation's decision?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> But Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul replied, “When I saw that the army had started to abandon me and that you didn’t come at the appointed time and that the Philistines had assembled at Micmash, <sup>12</sup> I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal and I have not sought the Lord’s favor.’ So I felt obligated to offer the burnt offering.” <sup>13</sup> Then Samuel said to Saul, “You have made a foolish choice! You have not obeyed the commandment that the Lord your God gave you. Had you done that, the Lord would have established your kingdom over Israel forever! <sup>14</sup> But now your kingdom will not continue! The Lord has sought out for himself a man who is loyal to him and the Lord has appointed him to be leader over his people, for you have not obeyed what the Lord commanded you.” <sup>24</sup> Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I have disobeyed what the Lord commanded and what you said as well. For I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in these passages?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul explains himself plainly: he saw the army scattering, Samuel hadn't arrived, the Philistines were massing at Micmash, and 'I felt obligated' to offer the sacrifice himself rather than wait. Later, about a different failure, he says it even more directly — 'I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.' In both cases, fear of losing his troops and his position pushed him to disobey a direct command from God, and it cost him the kingdom permanently. Saul's story shows that fear over safety can make us listen to the loudest pressure in the room instead of the command we already know we've been given.
elements.questionHint: Saul says outright, 'I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes' — whose voice ended up guiding his decision instead of God's command?

elements.sampleAnswer: Elijah has just seen God defeat the prophets of Baal, yet one threat from Jezebel sends him running for his life to Beer Sheba, and then further still into the desert alone. But fear doesn't stop at flight — it curdles into despair: 'I've had enough! Now, O Lord, take my life.' The same fear that made him run for safety now makes him want to give up on life altogether. It's a sobering picture of where unchecked fear can lead: not just away from danger, but into isolation and hopelessness, even after seeing God act powerfully just days before.
elements.questionHint: Elijah flees in fear and then almost immediately asks God to let him die — what does that jump from fear to despair reveal about where fear, left unchecked, can lead?

elements.passageText: <sup>69</sup> Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A slave girl came to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” <sup>70</sup> But he denied it in front of them all: “I don’t know what you’re talking about!” <sup>71</sup> When he went out to the gateway, another slave girl saw him and said to the people there, “This man was with Jesus the Nazarene.” <sup>72</sup> He denied it again with an oath, “I do not know the man!” <sup>73</sup> After a little while, those standing there came up to Peter and said, “You really are one of them too – even your accent gives you away!” <sup>74</sup> At that he began to curse, and he swore with an oath, “I do not know the man!” At that moment a rooster crowed.

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in these passages?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter's fear escalates step by step. First he simply denies it: 'I don't know what you're talking about.' Then he denies it again, this time 'with an oath.' By the third accusation he's cursing and swearing he doesn't know Jesus at all. Each time the danger of being associated with Jesus feels closer, Peter's denial gets more forceful, until he's willing to invoke a curse on himself to distance himself from the man he'd sworn to follow. Fear over his own safety doesn't just make him quiet — it makes him actively renounce the very relationship that defines him.
elements.questionHint: Track the escalation from a plain denial to swearing an oath to cursing — what does that pattern show about how far fear pushed Peter to protect himself?

elements.text:
Just as many dangerous lies contain a semblance of truth, so many dangerous relationships contain a semblance of safety. Here are some examples of corrupt, counterfeit, and/or exploitative versions of safety:

  • Prison: Security comes at the cost of freedom.
  • Parenting: parents should provide children with a safe zone, but sometimes this can drift towards becoming something like a prison (due to a lack of freedom). We need to remember that, in time, such prisons will be broken out of.
  • Political security: The desire for national security (perhaps in the face of terrorist threats) can be used as a reason to sacrifice freedom.
  • Job security: the desire for financial security can hold you hostage in a job that you might be wiser to move on from.
  • Controlling relationships: Some romantic partners will seem to offer security, but again at the cost of freedom.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Do not trust in princes, or in human beings, who cannot deliver! <sup>4</sup> Their life’s breath departs, they return to the ground; on that day their plans die.

elements.question: Why is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The warning is blunt: don't trust in princes. And the reason given, even in this short fragment, is mortality — 'their life's breath departs, they return to the ground.' Whatever power or protection a human ruler seems to offer, it comes from someone who is going to die like everyone else. A protector who can't outlast his own breath can't be the foundation of lasting safety. It's not that human leaders are useless or that we shouldn't respect them, but that placing our deepest trust for safety in anyone whose life will simply end one day is trusting something that was never built to hold that weight.
elements.questionHint: The passage points to the prince's 'life's breath' departing and his body returning 'to the ground' — what does that basic fact about mortality say about anyone's ability to be a lasting source of safety?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> So all the elders of Israel gathered together and approached Samuel at Ramah. <sup>5</sup> They said to him, “Look, you are old, and your sons don’t follow your ways. So now appoint over us a king to lead us, just like all the other nations have.” <sup>6</sup> But this request displeased Samuel, for they said, “Give us a king to lead us.” So Samuel prayed to the Lord. <sup>7</sup> The Lord said to Samuel, “Do everything the people request of you. For it is not you that they have rejected, but it is me that they have rejected as their king. <sup>8</sup> Just as they have done from the day that I brought them up from Egypt until this very day, they have rejected me and have served other gods. This is what they are also doing to you. <sup>9</sup> So now do as they say. But seriously warn them and make them aware of the policies of the king who will rule over them.” <sup>10</sup> So Samuel spoke all the words of the Lord to the people who were asking him for a king. <sup>11</sup> He said, “Here are the policies of the king who will rule over you: He will conscript your sons and put them in his chariot forces and in his cavalry; they will run in front of his chariot. <sup>12</sup> He will appoint for himself leaders of thousands and leaders of fifties, as well as those who plow his ground, reap his harvest, and make his weapons of war and his chariot equipment. <sup>13</sup> He will take your daughters to be ointment makers, cooks, and bakers. <sup>14</sup> He will take your best fields and vineyards and give them to his own servants. <sup>15</sup> He will demand a tenth of your seed and of the produce of your vineyards and give it to his administrators and his servants. <sup>16</sup> He will take your male and female servants, as well as your best cattle and your donkeys, and assign them for his own use. <sup>17</sup> He will demand a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will be his servants. <sup>18</sup> In that day you will cry out because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord won’t answer you in that day.” <sup>19</sup> But the people refused to heed Samuel’s warning. Instead they said, “No! There will be a king over us!”

elements.question: Why is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Israel asks for a king so they can be 'like all the other nations,' rejecting Samuel's leadership for something that looks more secure. But God tells Samuel plainly that the real rejection is aimed at him. Then Samuel spells out exactly what this 'safety' will cost: the king will take their sons for his army, their daughters for his household, their best fields, a tenth of their crops and flocks, until 'you yourselves will be his servants.' The very thing they sought for protection becomes the mechanism of their own exploitation. Seeking safety in the wrong source doesn't just disappoint — it can quietly reverse the relationship, so the shelter you begged for ends up owning you.
elements.questionHint: Look at the long list of things Samuel says the king will 'take' — sons, daughters, fields, servants, flocks. What's the irony in seeking safety through a king who ends up taking so much from the very people he's supposed to protect?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> “Do so because my people have committed a double wrong: they have rejected me, the fountain of life-giving water, and they have dug cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns which cannot even hold water.

elements.question: Why is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God names the problem as a double wrong: not just abandoning him, 'the fountain of life-giving water,' but replacing him with something that was never going to work anyway — cisterns they dug for themselves, and cracked ones at that, unable to even hold water. The image is almost comic in its wastefulness: they didn't just leave a good source for a mediocre one, they left an endless spring for a leaky hole they built by hand. That's what trusting the wrong thing for safety looks like — real effort poured into something that can't deliver what it promises, while the actual source of life sits rejected.
elements.questionHint: Compare the two water sources named here — a 'fountain of life-giving water' versus a 'cracked cistern which cannot even hold water.' What's the functional difference between them, beyond just who made them?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> “Do not accumulate for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal. <sup>20</sup> But accumulate for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup> For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

elements.question: Why is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus draws a stark contrast between two kinds of treasure: earthly treasure, which moth, rust, and thieves can all reach and destroy, versus treasure in heaven, which none of those forces can touch. Then he adds the key insight: 'where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.' It's not just that earthly security can be lost — it's that wherever we park our sense of safety, our heart follows and settles there too. If our treasure is something moths can eat or thieves can steal, our heart is tied to something fundamentally fragile, and we'll feel that fragility as constant, low-grade anxiety even when nothing has actually gone wrong yet.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says 'where your treasure is, there your heart will be also' — if your sense of safety is invested in something moth and rust can destroy, what happens to your heart as a result?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> Command those who are rich in this world’s goods not to be haughty or to set their hope on riches, which are uncertain, but on God who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment.

elements.question: What should we do instead, and why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's instruction has two parts that work together: don't be haughty or set your hope on riches, 'which are uncertain' — and instead set your hope on God, 'who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment.' The contrast is pointed: money is called uncertain, unstable ground to build a hope on, while God is described as the one who richly provides. The alternative to trusting wealth for safety isn't grim self-denial — it's redirecting that same hope toward a more reliable and, notably, more generous source. God isn't just described as sufficient here, but as one who provides abundantly, and for our enjoyment, not merely our survival.
elements.questionHint: The passage calls riches 'uncertain' but describes God as the one who 'richly provides.' What's the difference between hoping in something uncertain and hoping in someone described that way?

elements.text:
Case Study 10b - Help Jennifer Feel Safe

Mistake: It is likely a mistake to rebuke Jennifer for selfishness, to call her to sacrificial giving, or to stop being ’me’ focused, to care for others.

Gospel Angle: Jennifer’s key problem is that she doesn’t feel safe, and so she cannot (or will not) entrust herself to others. The way she sees life, people take from her, and people leave. She needs to hear of the God who has pursued her, her whole life, and who sees her as precious. The Father who sees her brokenness, sin and shortcoming, and who loves her still! The Son who gave up everything to become human and die for her. The Good Shepherd who walks with her and will never leave her, who loved her so much he laid down his life for her to bring her forgiveness.

She seems selfish because she grips everything in a tight fist. We can rebuke her and tell her to open the fist; we can try to pull things out of her clenched fist; or we can show her she is safe. If we show her she is safe - and if she accepts that truth - then one day, her hand will open wide.

Think of how to gain the trust of an abused dog - you don’t scold it; you sit with it and share your food with it. You show it that you are safe.

For her Pastor: Jennifer’s situation cannot be rushed. Words are cheap to her - she has trusted people and their words in the past, and they let her down. She feels shame about her selfishness, so rather than rebuke her further, empathise and show that we all struggle. Praise her for how she has raised Bobby, and encourage her for the strength she has shown to get through her difficulties in life. Remind her that God walks with her. He knows our weakness - the bruised reed he will not break.

For her Church: Resist asking Jennifer to serve. To someone else, this would be a great way to bring them on board and help them feel like they belong. To Jennifer, it just feels like more people are trying to take from her. Find ways for folk in the church to serve her where it’s clear there are no ’strings attached’. If she is unwell, have someone drop round food.

For her friends & family - Glen: Glen should keep reassuring her that he loves her and is here to stay. He could treat her to the beauty salon with his money, praise her for the times she looks out for others, or tell her how much he appreciates it when she shows kindness to him or others.

For her friends & family - Bobby: Bobby should assure her that no-one could ever replace her as his Mum. His girlfriend is different, she is not a threat or a rival to Jennifer. He wants to one day be the husband for a lady that his dad never was to Jennifer - Jennifer has raised him that way.

Case Study 11 - George (mid-20’s)

George comes looking for help. He says his life is a mess and thinks that God is ashamed of him. He’s been addicted to porn since he was a teenager, and he’s been struggling with depression on and off for a few years.

George’s Background

  • George also thinks he might be gay - he is drawn to homosexual porn, particularly involving older men.
  • He also suffers from panic attacks.
  • George is an ’arts-y, sensitive’ young man. He was born into a rural farming family. All of his brothers are natural farmers. He is not.
  • His father loves him but is impatient with George, he doesn’t understand why George is so lacking in the skills his father values, and so weak emotionally. His father thinks he needs to toughen him up with ’tough-love’. Since George was a young boy, his father would shout at him if he made a mistake and tell him to pull himself together when George cried. Once when George was 7 and he got himself in a state because he left a gate open letting the cattle out onto the road, his father got so angry with his crying that he screamed at George to ’shut up and stop being pathetic!’
  • George can tell his father is proud of his farming sons, but not him.
  • George is still living at home, he has a part-time job but also helps out on the farm whenever he is needed. Since the age of 18, when George works with his dad, he gets anxious and his anxiety has turned into panic attacks.

elements.text: We are intrinsically valuable, because God has made us so.

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> God created humankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them, male and female he created them.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This line is brief, but it's carrying enormous weight for something so short: God created humankind 'in his own image.' Value, in this account, isn't something humanity had to earn or grow into — it was built into the very act of being made. To bear someone's image is to carry a resemblance to them, a stamp that says something true about their worth is reflected in you. Long before anyone did anything to prove themselves useful or good, the simple fact of being made in God's own image already established their worth. That's the starting point Scripture gives for human value — not achievement, but origin.
elements.questionHint: The verse says humankind was made 'in his own image' — what does carrying someone's image, rather than just being one of their creations among many, suggest about the worth built into that?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> So then, just as sin entered the world through one man and death through sin, and so death spread to all people because all sinned –

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse is mostly setting up a comparison Paul doesn't finish until later in the chapter, but even on its own it tells us something significant: sin and death didn't stay contained to 'one man' — they spread 'to all people.' The scale of that consequence is striking. It means humanity isn't a random scattering of disconnected individuals whose choices don't matter beyond themselves; one man's action affected the entire human family. If our actions carry that kind of weight in God's ordered world, it says something about how seriously we're taken — significant enough that what happens to one person ripples through all of us.
elements.questionHint: The verse says death spread 'to all people' because of what happened through 'one man' — what does the scale of that consequence suggest about how much weight a single human life carries in God's world?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith. <sup>27</sup> For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. <sup>28</sup> There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female – for all of you are one in Christ Jesus. <sup>29</sup> And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to the promise.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up several categories that usually determine someone's worth or status — Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female — and says none of them count for defining who belongs to God's family: 'for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.' The basis for this new status isn't ancestry, class, or gender, but that 'you have clothed yourselves with Christ' through faith and baptism. Clothing yourself in someone changes how you're seen and identified. On that basis, believers become 'sons of God' and heirs of the promise made to Abraham — not by natural qualification, but by being placed into Christ himself.
elements.questionHint: Paul says believers have 'clothed yourselves with Christ' — what does putting on someone else's identity like clothing suggest about where your new value and status actually come from?

elements.text: God has given each of us an amazing set of gifts. That means we each have something to offer this world, an ability to make a difference. We often say that comparing ourselves to others is a bad idea and often it is, because we do it in a bad way. But there is a humble and grateful way that we can compare ourselves with others, so as to figure out how God has gifted us.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> For just as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body – though many – are one body, so too is Christ. <sup>13</sup> For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Whether Jews or Greeks or slaves or free, we were all made to drink of the one Spirit. <sup>14</sup> For in fact the body is not a single member, but many. <sup>15</sup> If the foot says, “Since I am not a hand, I am not part of the body,” it does not lose its membership in the body because of that. <sup>16</sup> And if the ear says, “Since I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,” it does not lose its membership in the body because of that. <sup>17</sup> If the whole body were an eye, what part would do the hearing? If the whole were an ear, what part would exercise the sense of smell? <sup>18</sup> But as a matter of fact, God has placed each of the members in the body just as he decided. <sup>19</sup> If they were all the same member, where would the body be? <sup>20</sup> So now there are many members, but one body.

elements.question: Why can we be confident our gifts matter?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul imagines the foot complaining, 'since I am not a hand, I am not part of the body,' and answers that its status in the body was never up for debate in the first place — 'it does not lose its membership in the body because of that.' The value of each part isn't determined by how prominent or central it looks, but by the simple fact that 'God has placed each of the members in the body just as he decided.' If every part were the same, the body couldn't even function — so the very differences that might make someone feel like the 'lesser' part are exactly what God arranged on purpose.
elements.questionHint: The foot's complaint is 'since I am not a hand, I am not part of the body' — according to the passage, does its membership in the body actually depend on being a hand?

elements.text: What are the gifts that God has given you, that he hasn’t given to everyone? How can you serve God well, as the person you are, with the gifts you have been given? Paying attention to our value as represented in the specific giftedness with which God has blessed us is not (necessarily) prideful. It can be done in a spirit of thankfulness.

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> Certainly you made my mind and heart; you wove me together in my mother’s womb. <sup>14</sup> I will give you thanks because your deeds are awesome and amazing. You knew me thoroughly;

elements.question: Are you just generically special or a precious ’one-off’ (& why)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist doesn't describe being manufactured on an assembly line — the language is intimate and individual: 'you wove me together in my mother's womb,' 'you made my mind and heart,' 'you knew me thoroughly.' Weaving is careful, attentive, one-at-a-time work, not mass production. This is what makes the psalmist respond with thanks rather than mere acknowledgment — 'your deeds are awesome and amazing.' You're not one of countless identical copies stamped out and shipped; you were personally formed and personally known before you ever did anything, which is exactly what makes you a precious one-off rather than just generically special among a crowd.
elements.questionHint: The psalm uses the word 'wove' for how you were made, and says God 'knew me thoroughly' — what does weaving, as opposed to stamping out identical copies, suggest about being one-of-a-kind rather than just generically special?

elements.text:
The significant people in the community around us - our family and friends, our colleagues and community leaders - can also help build up our understanding of our value when they tell us of that value, and even, simply, when they pay attention to us.

Feelings of being valueless come about if we allow ourselves to believe lies. These might be lies that we push onto ourselves, or others may try to push them onto us. They include statements like: ‘I’m no good at anything’ or ’I’m worthless’ or ’Nobody could love me’ or ’I do everything wrong.’ We must reject these lies.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> They do all their deeds to be seen by people, for they make their phylacteries wide and their tassels long. <sup>6</sup> They love the place of honor at banquets and the best seats in the synagogues    <sup>7</sup> and elaborate greetings in the marketplaces, and to have people call them ‘Rabbi.’

elements.question: How does seeking value in the wrong place lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus names the driving motive right at the start: 'they do all their deeds to be seen by people.' Everything that follows — wide phylacteries, long tassels, the best seats, elaborate greetings, being called 'Rabbi' — is aimed at an audience, not at God or genuine faithfulness. It's value sought through visibility and status symbols rather than character. The problem isn't that these things existed, but that they became performances calculated for maximum recognition. When value is chased this way, worth becomes dependent on being noticed, so the goal quietly shifts from being faithful to appearing impressive, which is a much shakier foundation for identity.
elements.questionHint: Jesus opens with 'they do all their deeds to be seen by people' — how does that one phrase explain everything else listed afterward, from wide phylacteries to loving the title 'Rabbi'?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> “Whenever you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, because they love to pray while standing in synagogues and on street corners so that people can see them. Truly I say to you, they have their reward.

elements.question: How does seeking value in the wrong place lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus is precise about the hypocrites' location and audience — praying 'standing in synagogues and on street corners so that people can see them.' The prayer isn't wrong in itself; what corrupts it is the intended viewer. And then comes the sobering line: 'they have their reward.' That's not a threat of future punishment so much as a statement of fact — the applause and notice they wanted is exactly what they got, and that's all they'll get. Seeking value in being seen by people means people's attention becomes the entire payment, closing off any deeper reward that could have come from being known by God instead.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says of those who pray to be seen, 'they have their reward' — reward from whom, and what deeper reward does chasing that one exclude?

elements.text: Dangerous relationships offer us a semblance of value without the reality. Flattery offers us attention at the cost of genuineness. The flatterer seems to affirm our value in their eyes, but without caring about what they really say. The ’value’ offered to us is superficial. Many young people are exploited by romantic partners smart enough to tell them what they want to hear, especially if the young person grew up in situations where they did not feel valued.

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup> How can you believe, if you accept praise from one another and don’t seek the praise that comes from the only God?

elements.question: Why is it bad to seek value and affirmation in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus links two things that might not seem connected at first: believing in him, and where you look for praise. 'How can you believe, if you accept praise from one another and don't seek the praise that comes from the only God?' Accepting human approval as your measure of worth isn't neutral — it actively competes with, and can crowd out, trust in God. If your sense of value is already satisfied by what people think of you, there's little room left to need or seek what God thinks. Seeking affirmation in the wrong place doesn't just leave you empty later; it can quietly block faith itself.
elements.questionHint: Jesus asks how someone can believe while they 'accept praise from one another' instead of seeking praise from God — what does chasing approval from people crowd out or compete with?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people, <sup>24</sup> because you know that you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward. Serve the Lord Christ.

elements.question: What is the alternative?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's alternative is simple to state but demanding to live: work at whatever you're doing 'with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people.' The audience shifts entirely — instead of performing for whoever's watching, the aim becomes pleasing Christ, who sees regardless of who else notices. And the payoff shifts too: 'you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward,' something secure and promised rather than fickle and dependent on human opinion. When Christ is the one you're ultimately serving, your worth and reward no longer rise and fall with whether anyone happened to notice or applaud.
elements.questionHint: Paul says to work 'as to the Lord and not for people' — whose reaction does your effort now answer to, and how does that change what you're actually working for?

elements.text: Evangelicals are good at explaining sin - and at telling people they are sinful. Evangelicals are not always so good at telling people they are precious. We are glorious ruins - broken, beautiful things. God created us for glory, and despite our fallenness, he has set his love on us. He has forgiven our sin, and he has chosen to delight in us.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> I thought, ‘Certainly you will respect me! Now you will accept correction!’ If she had done so, her home would not be destroyed by all the punishments I have threatened. But they eagerly sinned in everything they did.

elements.question: How would you respond to someone who says that God forgives us and then just patiently endures our failings?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's own words here push back hard against the idea of passive, endless tolerance. He says he expected correction to actually land — 'Now you will accept correction!' — with real consequences threatened if it didn't. But instead of turning, the people 'eagerly sinned in everything they did.' That word 'eagerly' matters: this isn't stumbling weakness God is patiently overlooking, it's willing, persistent rebellion. Someone who says God just forgives and endlessly endures our failings is missing this half of the picture — God does correct, does warn, and does respond to a refusal to change, even while remaining committed to his people.
elements.questionHint: Notice the word 'eagerly' describing how the people kept sinning even after correction was offered — what does that word suggest about the difference between struggling with sin and refusing to turn from it?

elements.text:
Case Study 11b - Help George know he’s valued

Mistake: In this situation, further ’tough love’ is unlikely to help George.

Gospel Angle: George needs to hear that he is special and unique, woven together in his mother’s womb. He needs to know that God loved him so much Christ died for him to forgive his sins. He needs to believe that God has seen George in his weakest most vulnerable state and yet God delights in him. There is no shame with God, he has cleansed us from our sins, we are clothed in Christ’s righteousness and beauty. God sees George exactly as he is - and God loves him. God has given each of us gifts. He has given George a unique set of gifts to bring blessing to those around him. He needs to know that ’ears aren’t blind.’ That’s the wrong way to look at people: ‘ears are designed to hear’. He needs to see that he has a purpose in this world, and to discover who God has designed him to be (and it’s not a farmer!), so that he can make a difference in this world to the glory of God.

For his Pastor: George needs someone to believe in him. Someone to help him explore who he is. His whole life, authority figures have told him he is a ’blind ear.’ There is a danger that, in the short term, an authority figure who shows George respect could be confusing for him, and sexual attraction could kick in. The pastor needs to avoid situations that could add to this interpretation, and also needs to not panic if there are signs of it.

For his Church: Give opportunities for George to explore and develop his gifts. Find an older man to mentor him, one who can encourage him and help him explore his gifts. In time teach George how he himself can become a mentor to younger men. In time, we want George to be able to see that he wasn’t pathetic as a boy, he just needed a compassionate authority figure to help him figure out who he was. Maybe George can be part of helping this be done for other young men, and maybe he can let Jesus do it for him.

For his Family & Friends: It is a tough call with family. It would be amazing if George’s father could appreciate who his son is, and not who he wants him to be. That is worth trying for, but it is also worth knowing in advance that it might be a hard perspective for George’s father to embrace. Much the same is true for his brothers also. As to the issue of living at home - if there is no progress, George might need to be encouraged to take the next step of independence and move out. But some confidence building might need to happen first.

In terms of safety, value, and belonging, George needs help with all three: he needs to feel safe, he needs to feel he is valued, and he needs to belong. Most especially, perhaps, he needs to feel valued. It is also important that he comes to know safety, value and belonging both vertically (with God) and horizontally (with other people). He needs to base his primary sense of safety, value, and belonging on the vertical (God), but he also needs support with the horizontal (from his pastor, his church, and - ideally - his family and friends).

Case Study 12 - Stanley & Debbie (late-30s)

Stanley is a farmer, he has been married for 12 years and has three children. His wife, Debbie, is pursuing divorce, she began the process a couple of years ago but Stanley talked her out of it. She thought he might change but he hasn’t and she is set on leaving him. Debbie says that Stanley is married to the farm, he is never in the house, they don’t go on dates, they don’t go on holiday together, he doesn’t spend any time with the kids unless they are working with him. Stanley says he is doing his best to provide for his family and do an honest day’s work. He knows he should spend more time with his wife and kids and he desperately doesn’t want to lose them, but every time they have an argument about it, he makes an effort to be present in the home but it soon fades away. Debbie has had enough.

Stanley’s Background

  • Stanley was brought up in a loving Christian home as a child. He loves and respects his father & mother. His Dad often pops down to the farm to give him a hand and Stanley loves spending time with him working.
  • He doesn’t go to church much and struggles to respect the local minister of the church. He says, ‘It’s hard to listen to someone who hasn’t done a hard day’s work in his life.’
  • Stanley gets on well with his oldest son, who is a natural farmer and loves the work. The middle son and Stanley don’t get on so well. The middle son would rather meet up with his friends on a Saturday than join in with the farm work. Sometimes Stanley can belittle him for being lazy.
  • Stanley loves his father and looks up to him. When Stanley was 11, he was riding in the tractor with his Dad and on the road they got stuck behind traffic going to the local football match, some flashy BMW cars were in front of them and he saw his father get visibly agitated. His father said to Stanley: ‘Look at those wasters. They drive around enjoying themselves, spending their days watching football, probably living off the government, or their rich parents. It’s people like that that are destroying our country, they couldn’t do a day’s work if their life depended on it. They make me sick.’

To be loved but not known is comforting but superficial. To be known and not loved is our greatest fear. But to be fully known and truly loved is, well, a lot like being loved by God.
Tim Keller

Until you conquer the fear of being an outsider, an outsider you will remain.
C.S. Lewis
