elements.text: We all want to belong, and ultimately, we belong to God.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from your enslavement to the Egyptians.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God states the terms of this belonging in his own voice: 'I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be your God.' Notice who's doing the acting — God takes, God commits to being their God — and notice where they're being taken from: 'your enslavement to the Egyptians.' This isn't a relationship Israel earned or negotiated; it's one God initiated out of slavery, on his own terms and by his own choice. That's the ground for confidence — belonging to God rests on his decision to claim a people for himself, not on their track record of deserving it.
elements.questionHint: Look at who is doing the taking in 'I will take you to myself' — and what condition they were being taken out of. Whose initiative creates this belonging?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> Then you will again be my people and I will be your God.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The promise is short, but it echoes a relationship that had been broken: 'you will again be my people and I will be your God.' That word 'again' matters — this isn't the first time this bond existed; it had been disrupted, and God is the one restoring it. Belonging here isn't described as something Israel rebuilds through effort, but as a covenant God himself renews and re-declares. The simplicity of the formula — my people, your God — is itself the point: after everything that went wrong, the relationship comes back to this same basic, mutual claim.
elements.questionHint: The verse says 'you will AGAIN be my people' — what does that word imply about the history of this relationship, and who is the one restoring it?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> And when you heard the word of truth (the gospel of your salvation) – when you believed in Christ – you were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup> who is the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul uses two images here that both point toward security rather than uncertainty. Believers are 'marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit' — a seal being a mark of ownership and authenticity — and that same Spirit is 'the down payment of our inheritance,' a partial payment that guarantees the rest is coming. Belonging to God isn't left as a hope we can't verify; it's sealed and backed by a deposit already given. The full inheritance is still ahead, 'until the redemption of God's own possession,' but the Spirit's presence now is the proof that the rest of the promise is coming.
elements.questionHint: The passage uses two financial and legal images — 'seal' and 'down payment' — what do a mark of ownership and a partial payment guaranteeing the rest both say about how secure this belonging is?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are God’s children. <sup>17</sup> And if children, then heirs (namely, heirs of God and also fellow heirs with Christ) – if indeed we suffer with him so we may also be glorified with him.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes a kind of double confirmation here: 'the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children.' It's not just an outward legal fact declared once and left unfelt — it's something testified to from within, alongside our own awareness. And the identity carries real consequence: 'if children, then heirs,' co-heirs with Christ himself. Belonging to God isn't a fragile hope we're left to talk ourselves into; it's something the Spirit actively affirms, paired with the sober reality that sharing in Christ's sufferings now is bound up with sharing in his glory later.
elements.questionHint: Paul says the Spirit 'bears witness WITH our spirit' — what does having two witnesses, rather than just one, suggest about how certain this claim to belong to God is meant to feel?

elements.text:
In human relationships, we feel we belong when we know we are part of something bigger than ourselves, when we can recognise meaning and purpose to our role within the community, and when we feel accepted - that it is safe to be seen by others. We feel we belong when we feel at ’home’ with people, when we feel part of a community, when we feel connected to others.

The opposite is also true. If these factors are missing, you won’t feel that you belong. For example, you’ll struggle to belong if you are seen as the ’Black Sheep’ of the family, or if you feel isolated from others or rejected by others, or if you feel you have to hide who you are to blend in, or if you question what your place in this world is.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a brave warrior. His mother was a prostitute, but Gilead was his father. <sup>2</sup> Gilead’s wife also gave him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they made Jephthah leave and said to him, “You are not going to inherit any of our father’s wealth, because you are another woman’s son.” <sup>3</sup> So Jephthah left his half-brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Lawless men joined Jephthah’s gang and traveled with him.

elements.question: When Jephthah is rejected, what sort of community does he find?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jephthah's own family shuts him out — his half-brothers tell him plainly, 'you are not going to inherit any of our father's wealth, because you are another woman's son,' and drive him away. Rejected by the community that should have claimed him, he doesn't end up alone; he finds belonging among 'lawless men' who join his gang in the land of Tob. It's real community, in the sense that people gather around him, but it's a community formed out of shared exclusion and lawlessness rather than health or honor. Rejection by the right people doesn't erase the need to belong — it often just redirects it toward whoever will take you in.
elements.questionHint: Notice who exactly joins Jephthah once his family casts him out — 'lawless men.' What does the kind of community he finds say about what happens when someone is rejected by the people who should have claimed him?

elements.text: Dangerous relationships may offer us a semblance of belonging, but without the reality of true belonging. Peer pressure tempts you to belong at the cost of authenticity - succumbing to things that go against your values, in order to belong. Diversity is not celebrated, and you are told (implicitly or explicitly) that you have to conform to a certain standard in order to belong. Authenticity is not valued, and it is not safe to be seen for who you really are.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test and approve what is the will of God – what is good and well-pleasing and perfect.

elements.question: What is the alternative to this sort of wrong conformity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a direct line between two options: being 'conformed to this present world,' shaped from the outside by pressure to fit its pattern, or being 'transformed by the renewing of your mind,' changed from the inside out. The alternative to wrong conformity isn't just resisting the crowd through willpower — it's a genuine renewal of how you think, which then equips you to 'test and approve what is the will of God.' Belonging that comes from conforming to the world is passive and externally imposed; the transformation Paul calls for actively reshapes your thinking so your choices flow from renewed conviction rather than social pressure.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts being 'conformed' to the world with being 'transformed' by renewed thinking — which one starts from the outside pressing in, and which one starts from the inside out?

elements.text: Slightly different is the temptation to join the crowd and lose yourself. Going with the flow of the people around you, and abdicating your own responsibility. Another temptation is to find belonging by excluding others. Some groups make their members feel superior by keeping others away. When a fellowship is working well, the mutual love it embodies overflows to draw others in. When a fellowship is not working well, it tries to keep others out. This form of negative fellowship is not based on love, but on power and exclusion.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> “You must not follow a crowd in doing evil things; in a lawsuit you must not offer testimony that agrees with a crowd so as to pervert justice,

elements.question: How does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The command is specific and practical: don't follow a crowd into evil, and in a lawsuit, don't shape your testimony to match what the majority wants to hear just because it's the majority. The danger named here isn't belonging itself, but what belonging can quietly cost — 'so as to pervert justice.' Going along with a group, even a large or confident one, can pull a person into dishonesty or injustice they wouldn't choose on their own. This is a clear warning that the pull to belong and agree with the crowd can override what's actually true and right, if we let it.
elements.questionHint: The passage warns against testimony that 'agrees with a crowd so as to pervert justice' — what does that phrase suggest is at risk when belonging to the group becomes more important than telling the truth?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I have disobeyed what the Lord commanded and what you said as well. For I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.

elements.question: How does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul's confession is unusually direct about his motive: 'I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.' He doesn't blame confusion or bad information — he names fear of the group's disapproval, and his desire to stay in step with them, as the reason he disobeyed a command he already knew. Wanting to belong to and please the army pulled harder on him than his loyalty to what God had said. It's a plain example of how the pull to fit in with the people around us can override obedience, even when we already know exactly what we were supposed to do.
elements.questionHint: Saul says plainly, 'I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes' — what did he choose to belong to instead of obeying the command he already knew?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he had clearly done wrong.  <sup>12</sup> Until certain people came from James, he had been eating with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he stopped doing this and separated himself because he was afraid of those who were pro-circumcision. <sup>13</sup> And the rest of the Jews also joined with him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led astray with them by their hypocrisy.

elements.question: How does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter had been eating openly with Gentile believers, living out the truth that in Christ there's no longer a barrier between Jew and Gentile. But 'when certain people came from James,' he pulled back and separated himself, and Paul names the reason without softening it: 'he was afraid of those who were pro-circumcision.' Wanting to stay in good standing with one group led Peter to abandon a deeper belonging he already knew was true, and it was contagious — 'even Barnabas was led astray with them.' Fear of losing approval from the wrong crowd can pull even mature believers into behavior that betrays what they actually believe.
elements.questionHint: Paul says Peter changed his behavior specifically 'when they arrived' and because 'he was afraid of those who were pro-circumcision' — whose approval was he protecting, and what truer belonging did it cost him?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Acknowledge that the Lord is God! He made us and we belong to him; we are his people, the sheep of his pasture.

elements.question: What should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm puts the order in a way worth noticing: 'He made us and we belong to him.' Belonging follows directly from being made — it isn't something we constructed for ourselves or negotiated after the fact. The image that follows, 'we are his people, the sheep of his pasture,' reinforces the same idea: sheep don't establish their own belonging to a shepherd, they simply are his, cared for and led. When we're tempted to look elsewhere for a sense of belonging, this is the plain fact worth returning to — we already belong to the one who made us, before we do anything to secure it.
elements.questionHint: The psalm says 'He made us and we belong to him' — which comes first in that sentence, the making or the belonging, and what does that order suggest about how this belonging was established?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now, this is what the Lord says, the one who created you, O Jacob, and formed you, O Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I will protect you. I call you by name, you are mine.

elements.question: What should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This portion of the verse only gives us the opening formula — 'this is what the Lord says' — the introduction to a declaration whose actual content isn't included here. Even so, it's worth noticing what this small phrase does say: whatever follows is presented as coming directly and personally from the Lord himself, not as secondhand report or general wisdom. It sets up an announcement worth waiting for and trusting because of who is speaking it. The reminder we're meant to hold onto is that when God speaks to identity and belonging, it is genuinely his own voice addressing us, not a rumor about him.
elements.questionHint: This phrase is only the introduction — 'this is what the Lord says' — whose voice is being announced here, even before we hear what's actually said?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> So then you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household,

elements.question: What should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul marks a clear before-and-after: no longer 'foreigners and noncitizens,' but 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.' Both new categories describe full belonging rather than partial or provisional status. Citizenship implies legal standing and rights within a community, not just permission to visit it; being part of a household implies the intimacy of family, not just formal membership. Put together, the reminder is layered — you belong civically, among God's people, and relationally, within his own family — which leaves no room for the old status of outsider looking in from a distance.
elements.questionHint: Paul moves from 'foreigners and noncitizens' to 'fellow citizens' and 'members of God's household' — what two different kinds of belonging (civic and then relational) do those final two terms describe?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But you are a chosen race , a royal priesthood , a holy nation , a people of his own , so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.

elements.question: What should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter stacks up four identity titles in a row — 'a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own' — each one describing a group set apart and claimed, not a collection of individuals figuring things out alone. And then he gives the reason for it: 'so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.' Belonging here isn't just a private comfort to enjoy quietly; it comes with a purpose. Being called into this identity is meant to result in a community that shows and tells what the one who called them out of darkness is actually like.
elements.questionHint: Peter piles up four titles — 'chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, a people of his own' — and then gives a purpose clause, 'so that you may proclaim...' What is this belonging ultimately for?

elements.text:
Case Study 12b - Tell Stanley a better story

Aged 11, Stanley saw the look in his father’s eyes - the anger and disgust as he looked at those people. Stanley never wanted his father to look at him that way, and this fear shaped him. Unconsciously he began to fear that maybe he was a waster and that his dad would look at him with those eyes. He put his hope in hard work to win his dad’s respect. As a teenager he avoided TV, or going out with his mates. He worked late on the farm. He feared that if his dad ever really saw him, he’d see him as a waster, and look at him with those eyes. Hard work became his only hope. He spent the rest of his life running from that look. When he married and had kids, he loved them dearly, but he was still running. If he stopped to play with the kids, or take his wife out, his dad’s look would chase him. The farm was the only safe place. Stanley was hiding from himself, from everyone - scared that they would see him as a waster. Scared of those eyes. Yes, Stanley would look at Christ, but he was scared to let Christ look deep into his soul. To flourish, he needs to let Jesus in. He needs to watch Jesus take his 11-year-old self by the hand, as He speaks these words:

Your father loves you to bits. He has been through a lot and he is hurting. He has worked so hard his whole life and money has always been tight. He wanted to provide enough for his family, but when he couldn’t he began to hate himself, and in his pain, bitterness started to grow towards others who had an easy life. One day you saw that bitterness in his eyes, when he looked at those people in the fancy cars on the way to the football. That day you saw a look that left a scar on your soul. You feared that one day your dad would look at you that same way. But Stanley, I want you to see past the look and see your father’s pain. That look was not about you, it was about his struggles. In his pain, bitterness got a foothold, and that day it jumped from his eyes into your soul and you have been running ever since. That bitterness has put shadows in your soul and in your family. It has cost you peace in your soul, peace in your family, and it will cost you your farm. Your worth is not measured by how much you work. Your father loves you and your Heavenly Father loves you, I love you. I see your pain and I see your brokenness, I see the darkness in your soul that you are scared to look at, and I want to make this my home. I am here, in your heart to stay. I want you to see my eyes, as I look on you. I see the beauty within brokenness, you are loved, we are home, you don’t need to run any more.

When Stanley allows Jesus to gaze on him, he can stop running from his father’s eyes. He can spend time with the people he loves, enjoying the eyes of grace.

Case Study 13 - Andrew (mid-30s)

Andrew has been following Christ for the last five years. Before coming to faith, he lived a life that he’s not proud of. His past is filled with mistakes, including broken relationships, wasted opportunities, substance abuse, and decisions that hurt others. When Andrew accepted Christ, he experienced a massive sense of forgiveness and hope. For the first time in years, he felt free from his guilt and shame. He was baptised, and his church welcomed him warmly, reminding him that he is now a child of God.

However, as time has passed, Andrew has struggled to fully embrace his new identity. He finds himself haunted by memories of his past and feels that others, especially those who knew him before he became a Christian, still see him as the same old person. Although he is growing in his faith, reading the Bible, and attending church, Andrew sometimes feels like his old life is following him around. He wonders, ‘Am I really that different? Or am I just pretending to have changed?’

Andrew often feels discouraged, especially when he faces temptations or falls into old habits of thinking - or worse, when he relapses into old sins. (He is thankful this is becoming less frequent - but regularly depressed that he still falls into some of his old ways of behaving.)

He knows in his head that he has been born again, and is a child of God and a new creation in Christ - but his heart finds it difficult to believe that his past no longer defines him.

When Jesus rose again, God’s new creation emerged from the tomb, introducing a new way of being human, a new creation in which the broken pieces of the world are being put back together.
N.T. Wright

You are no longer what you used to be. You are a new creature in Christ. Your outward existence is the same, but your inner nature is marvellously changed.
Charles Spurgeon

elements.text: Central to understanding who we are in Christ, is understanding that we have been made new in him.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will remove the heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God promises to give a new heart and put a new spirit within us, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh. This isn't a minor tune-up — it's a transplant. A heart of stone is unresponsive, hard, resistant to God; a heart of flesh is soft, alive, able to feel and respond to him. Being new in Christ means the very core of who we are — our desires, our capacity to love and obey — has been exchanged for something that can actually beat in rhythm with God, not just externally reformed but internally remade.
elements.questionHint: What's the difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh — what can one do that the other can't?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul ties our newness to Christ's own resurrection: because we've been buried with him through baptism, we're raised to walk in "a new life," just as Christ was raised through the Father's glory. Being new in Christ isn't just forgiveness for the old life — it's participation in a death and a resurrection. The old identity was buried; a new way of living, patterned after resurrection power rather than the old patterns, has begun. It's not self-improvement; it's new life on the other side of death.
elements.questionHint: The verse links our "new life" to something specific that happened to Christ through the Father's glory — what was it, and why would our new life need to be modeled on that?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> So then, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; what is old has passed away – look, what is new has come!

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul states it as plainly as possible: anyone in Christ is "a new creation" — what is old has passed away, and what is new has come. Notice the totality of the language: not improved, not patched up, but a whole new creation, with the old genuinely gone. This is one of the clearest ways we are new in Christ — our identity isn't defined by our past record or old patterns anymore, but by being remade into something that didn't exist before.
elements.questionHint: The verse uses two strong contrasts — "passed away" and "has come." What do those words suggest about how complete this change is meant to be?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage is careful to say what our newness is NOT based on: not "works of righteousness that we have done." Instead it comes "through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit," and it flows from God's mercy. So one way we're new in Christ is through a Spirit-worked rebirth and renewal that we receive rather than earn — it's God's washing and renewing at work in us, not our own performance record.
elements.questionHint: The passage explicitly rules out one possible source for our salvation before naming the real one — what does it rule out, and what does it put in its place?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By his great mercy he gave us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter praises God because "by his great mercy he gave us new birth into a living hope," and that new birth comes specifically through the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. So this is another facet of our newness: we've been born again, not into ordinary hope but a "living hope" — a hope that is alive because it's rooted in a risen Christ rather than mere wishful thinking. Our newness includes this fresh, resurrection-powered hope that didn't exist before.
elements.questionHint: The passage calls this a "living hope" rather than just "hope" — what does the resurrection have to do with why this hope is alive rather than just wishful?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. So the life I now live in the body, I live because of the faithfulness of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes his newness almost paradoxically: "I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." Being new in Christ, here, means an exchange of who is at the center — the old self was crucified, and now Christ himself lives in Paul. Even the ongoing life Paul lives "in the body" is lived by the faithfulness of the Son of God who loved him. Our newness includes this indwelling — Christ living his life through us.
elements.questionHint: Paul says it's "no longer I who live, but Christ" — what does it mean for Christ to actually live IN a person, rather than the person just trying harder to follow him?

elements.text: Jesus does not just ’patch us up.’ The corruption we face, because of sin, is much bigger than any ’patch-up’ could fix. But thankfully, the salvation Jesus brings to us is even greater than the depths of our sin.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Jesus replied, “I tell you the solemn truth, unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

elements.question: Why is it so important that we are made new in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes it an absolute condition: "unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." This is why our newness matters so much — it isn't a bonus or an optional upgrade, it's the very thing that determines whether we can see and enter God's kingdom at all. No amount of moral effort in our old, unborn state gets us there; only being born from above does. Being made new in Christ is important because without it, the kingdom is literally invisible to us.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't say the unborn-again person struggles to see the kingdom — what stronger word does he use, and what does that tell you about how essential this new birth is?

elements.text: Sin is big, but salvation is bigger. That’s why we need a radical new start. But we must be clear: God doesn’t love us because we are good - it’s the other way round: God makes us good because He loves us.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> for you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God. <sup>5</sup> So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry.

elements.question: Is our old self something that is dead, or needs to die, or both?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Both, and the passage holds them together without smoothing out the tension. Verse 3 states a finished fact: "you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God" — in Christ's death, our old self already died. But verse 5 gives a command: "put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth" — sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed. So our old self is dead in the sense that its power has been broken, but it still shows up in specific practices we're responsible to actively kill.
elements.questionHint: One verse is stated as something already true about you ("you have died"), the other as something you're told to do ("put to death") — how can both be accurate at once?

elements.text: Christ died for us, in our place, to bring us to God. He was raised from the dead, to begin a new creation, and to make us new. We have not yet been taken to the New Heavens and the New Earth. We still live in this present evil age. That’s why there is a call, as well as a proclamation: we need to keep putting to death the old nature that is now dead through Christ. We are to be as different from our old selves as light is from darkness - and yet this difference does not happen by remote control. We are called to take an active part in the transformation.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> Do not lie to one another since you have put off the old man with its practices <sup>10</sup> and have been clothed with the new man that is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage names lying specifically — "do not lie to one another" — as something tied to "the old man" we've put off. In its place we've been "clothed with the new man that is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it." So one old thing to get rid of is dishonesty between believers, precisely because it belongs to a self we've already taken off, like an old garment, in favor of one being continually renewed into the image of our Creator.
elements.questionHint: What specific old habit does Paul name here as something that belongs to "the old man" and doesn't fit the "new man"?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> We know that our old man was crucified with him so that the body of sin would no longer dominate us, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says "our old man was crucified with him so that the body of sin would no longer dominate us." The old thing to get rid of, or rather recognize as already dealt with, is sin's dominating power over us — the passage's goal is precisely that we would "no longer be enslaved to sin." Our old, sin-enslaved self was put to death with Christ so that sin's mastery over us is broken, not so we'd keep serving the same master out of habit.
elements.questionHint: The verse gives a purpose ("so that…") for the old man's crucifixion — what result was it meant to produce in how sin relates to us now?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> Now those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Short and direct: "those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." What we're to get rid of here is "the flesh" — not just isolated bad actions but the whole cluster of passions and desires that drive them. Belonging to Christ is tied directly to this crucifixion; it's presented as already true of those who are his, meaning our fleshly passions and desires have lost their claim on us, even though we still have to live that reality out.
elements.questionHint: The verse pairs "the flesh" with two other words — what are they, and what do they add to what exactly gets crucified?

elements.text: The very centre of who we are is being renewed, so that we take on the character of Christ. New birth doesn’t ’improve’ our old nature, it gives us a new nature, a new capacity to put on Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> You were taught with reference to your former way of life to lay aside the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires, <sup>23</sup> to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, <sup>24</sup> and to put on the new man who has been created in God’s image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage lays out the whole sequence: lay aside "the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires," be "renewed in the spirit of your mind," and then "put on the new man who has been created in God's image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth." So what we put on instead is this new man — an identity actually created in God's image, marked by righteousness and holiness that flow from truth rather than the deceit that corrupted the old one.
elements.questionHint: The passage contrasts "deceitful desires" corrupting the old man with something else the new man's righteousness "comes from" — what is that source?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> But sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of wrong desires. For apart from the law, sin is dead.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse doesn't describe the new thing we put on — instead it exposes why relying on the law alone never gets us there. Paul says "sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of wrong desires." The command itself was good, but sin hijacked it to stir up exactly the desires it forbade. That's the trap: fighting the old self by willpower and rule-keeping alone gives sin something to grab onto. It points us toward needing something other than the law itself — a Spirit-renewed life rather than sheer rule-following.
elements.questionHint: The verse says sin "seized the opportunity" through the commandment — what does that reveal about why simply having a rule to follow isn't enough to change us?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test and approve what is the will of God – what is good and well-pleasing and perfect.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's answer here is to "be transformed by the renewing of your mind" instead of being "conformed to this present world." What we put on instead of worldly conformity is a mind actively being renewed — one capable of testing and approving what God's will is, described as "good and well-pleasing and perfect." It's a call to let our whole way of thinking be remade, so that discerning and doing God's will becomes possible rather than just following the world's mold by default.
elements.questionHint: The verse contrasts being "conformed" with being "transformed" — what's the difference between those two words, and which one involves the mind being renewed?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> For we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Here the answer is good works — but rooted in a specific identity: "we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works." What we put on instead of the old life is a life of doing the good works God "prepared beforehand so we may do them." These aren't works we invent to earn favor; they're works already planned by God for us specifically, because we are his handiwork, newly made in Christ for exactly this purpose.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God "prepared beforehand" these good works — what does that timing suggest about whose idea the good works are, and whose we are as we do them?

elements.text:
Case Study 13b - Andrew (mid-30s)

Being made new in Christ is not a minor adjustment - it’s a total transformation. Anyone who is in Christ is a ’new creation.’ The old has gone, and the new has come. This means that Andrew is no longer defined by the mistakes he made in his past. Andrew needs to meditate on these truths until they dwell within him and begin to shape him. But this new life doesn’t happen automatically, without effort. For Andrew, this means recognising that his past mistakes no longer define him, but it also means actively working to let go of the habits, mindsets, and behaviours that belonged to his old life.

Andrew feels like his past is still following him around, but this is exactly why the Bible tells us to continually ’put off’ the old self and ’put on’ the new self. Every time Andrew resists temptations to fall into old patterns, he is living out his new identity in Christ. This doesn’t mean the old struggles will disappear instantly, but it does mean that Andrew has the power, through the Holy Spirit, to walk in newness of life.

Andrew needs to internalise the truth that God’s work in him is ongoing. He may still feel the weight of his past and the pull of old habits, but God is continually at work transforming him to be more like Christ. He can take comfort in knowing that being a new creation is not about never making mistakes - it’s about living in the assurance that God’s grace enables him to keep growing. God will never abandon him. He is faithfully working in Andrew’s life, even when progress feels slow.

Andrew can take steps to help himself fully embrace his new identity: Dwelling in the truth of God’s Word, especially the truth of his new identity in Christ, will help that truth dwell in him. Andrew might also benefit from connecting with a Christian mentor or accountability partner who can encourage him in his walk and remind him of his new identity when he’s feeling discouraged. Having someone to pray with and share struggles with can really help. Andrew needs to consciously surrender any lingering shame from his past to God. He can do this through prayer, asking God to help him release the weight of his old mistakes and to live in the freedom of being forgiven and made new. Each time Andrew chooses to live in a way that reflects his new identity - whether it’s showing kindness, resisting temptation, or making choices that honour God - he is ’putting on’ the new self. He can look for ways to actively practice living out this new creation, asking God for strength each day. His new life is a reflection of the resurrection power that raised Jesus from the dead.

Case Study 14 - Hannah (late 20s)

Hannah has been a believer for most of her life. She attends church regularly, listens to sermons, and volunteers for occasional events. But even though she has been involved for years, Hannah often feels like she doesn’t really belong in her church community. She’s friendly with people at church, but she hasn’t formed any deep relationships. Sometimes, she wonders if anyone would even notice if she stopped attending.

Recently, Hannah has been wrestling with a growing sense of isolation. While she enjoys her personal relationship with Christ, she has been noticing more and more that she doesn’t feel deeply connected to her church family. Every Sunday, she hears about being part of the body of Christ, but in practice, she feels like a distant spectator. When her pastor talks about community and serving one another, Hannah feels guilty for not being more involved, but she also feels unsure about how to take the next step. ’Isn’t it enough to just come to church and be a good Christian?’ she asks herself.

Hannah wants to experience the kind of deep, meaningful relationships she hears about in the Bible, but she isn’t sure how to make that happen.

The church is not a museum for saints, but a hospital for sinners. We are the living embodiment of the risen Christ in the world.
N.T. Wright

The body of Christ is a community of the redeemed, and our membership in it is by God’s grace. We live not as independent individuals but as members of one another.
Eugene Peterson

We need to recognize that we are not just members of a church; we are members of the body of Christ, and that identity shapes everything about our lives.
Paul David Tripp

elements.text: The church does not exist to promote religion. It is Christ’s body - that means it is his physical presence here in this world, it is called to be the agent of God’s mission here in this world.

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup> People do not light a lamp and put it under a basket but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup> In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they can see your good deeds and give honor to your Father in heaven.

elements.question: What mission did Jesus give to his followers?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells his followers plainly, "You are the light of the world," comparing them to a city on a hill that can't be hidden, or a lamp meant to be put on a stand rather than under a basket. The mission that follows is direct: "let your light shine before people, so that they can see your good deeds and give honor to your Father in heaven." Our mission is visibility, not concealment — living in a way that our good deeds are seen, with the aim not of our own praise but of pointing people to God.
elements.questionHint: Jesus gives two images for what light is NOT supposed to do (hidden, under a basket) — what does that tell you about the kind of visibility he expects from his followers?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> And let us take thought of how to spur one another on to love and good works,  <sup>25</sup> not abandoning our own meetings, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging each other, and even more so because you see the day drawing near.

elements.question: What does the Bible say about Christians meeting together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage tells us to "take thought of how to spur one another on to love and good works," explicitly warning against "abandoning our own meetings, as some are in the habit of doing." Instead we're to keep "encouraging each other," and to do so with increasing urgency "because you see the day drawing near." Meeting together isn't presented as optional or merely social — it's a deliberate practice of mutual encouragement toward love and good works, made more important, not less, as time goes on.
elements.questionHint: The passage names a habit some people had fallen into regarding meetings — what was it, and what are believers told to do instead?

elements.text:
Being a member of a local church is no optional extra for Christians. It is essential to our identity as followers of Christ.

As disciples of Christ, we are bound to Christ, and therefore bound to one another in the love of God; our lives are intertwined as we seek to follow Christ together.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> For just as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body – though many – are one body, so too is Christ. <sup>13</sup> For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Whether Jews or Greeks or slaves or free, we were all made to drink of the one Spirit. <sup>14</sup> For in fact the body is not a single member, but many.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a direct comparison: "just as the body is one and yet has many members... so too is Christ." Being a member of Christ's body means belonging to one unified whole made up of genuinely different parts, and that unity was created "in one Spirit... baptized into one body," erasing old dividing lines between "Jews or Greeks or slaves or free." Membership isn't uniformity — "the body is not a single member, but many" — but a diversity of parts joined by one Spirit into one body.
elements.questionHint: Paul says the body was formed "in one Spirit" across categories like Jew, Greek, slave, and free — what does that tell you about what actually unites members of Christ's body?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> For just as in one body we have many members, and not all the members serve the same function, <sup>5</sup> so we who are many are one body in Christ, and individually we are members who belong to one another.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul again uses the body image, noting that "not all the members serve the same function," yet "we who are many are one body in Christ." Being a member means two things held together: individuality of function — you're not interchangeable with every other member — and genuine belonging to one another, since he says members are those "who belong to one another." Being part of Christ's body means your distinct role matters precisely because you're bound to others who need it.
elements.questionHint: The passage says members "serve" different functions but also "belong to one another" — how do those two ideas work together rather than against each other?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> It was he who gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, <sup>12</sup> to equip the saints for the work of ministry, that is, to build up the body of Christ, <sup>13</sup> until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God – a mature person, attaining to the measure of Christ’s full stature.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage shows that Christ gave specific people — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers — with a purpose: "to equip the saints for the work of ministry" and "build up the body of Christ." Being a member of Christ's body means being someone these gifted people are meant to equip, moving all of us together "until we all attain to the unity of the faith... a mature person, attaining to the measure of Christ's full stature." Membership carries a growth trajectory — toward unity and maturity, not just belonging as a static fact.
elements.questionHint: The gifted leaders in this passage aren't meant to do all the ministry themselves — what are they given "to equip" others for?

elements.text: Bodies are interdependent, not independent. If you saw a severed ear lying on the road, you would not think, ‘Oh, look! There’s an independent ear, striking out on its own. Good for it!’ You would recognise that there had been some tragedy. Ears do not do well lying ’independently’ on the road. Nor do Christians do well, striking out ’independently’ from the body of Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> So then you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, <sup>20</sup> because you have been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. <sup>21</sup> In him the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, <sup>22</sup> in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage moves through several pictures at once: we're no longer "foreigners and noncitizens" but "fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household." That household is also described as a building — "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone" — growing into "a holy temple" and "a dwelling place of God in the Spirit." Belonging to God's household means moving from outsider status to full membership in a structure that God himself is actively building and living in.
elements.questionHint: The passage says we're no longer "foreigners and noncitizens" — what are we instead, and what is Christ's specific role in the building we now belong to?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> you yourselves, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood and to offer spiritual sacrifices that are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls believers "living stones" being "built up as a spiritual house," with the purpose of being "a holy priesthood" who "offer spiritual sacrifices that are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." Belonging to God's household here means being actual building material — alive, not inert — assembled into a house whose function is priestly: offering sacrifices, though now spiritual ones, made acceptable only through Jesus. Household membership comes with a job: worship that is welcomed by God because of Christ.
elements.questionHint: Peter calls believers "living stones" rather than just stones — what does the word "living" add, and what is the finished structure used for?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> But Christ is faithful as a son over God’s house. We are of his house, if in fact we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope we take pride in.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage draws a contrast between Christ, who is "faithful as a son over God's house," and us: "we are of his house." But it attaches a condition — "if in fact we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope we take pride in." Belonging to God's household here isn't just a title we passively hold; it's tied to continuing to hold firmly to our confidence and hope in Christ, the faithful Son who rules over that house.
elements.questionHint: The verse adds a small but important word — "if" — before naming what we need to hold onto. What are we told to hold firmly to?

elements.text: We often first turn to Christ individually, in repentance and faith. But we are not called to follow Christ individually. We are part of something greater, a household built on the foundation of Christ. This household is where we learn what it means to love and be loved, to serve and be served.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own, so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. <sup>10</sup> You once were not a people , but now you are God’s people. You were shown no mercy, but now you have received mercy.

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter names our identity in a cluster of titles — "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own" — and immediately attaches a purpose clause: "so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." Our royal priesthood identity isn't just status; it comes with a mission to declare God's excellencies. That mission makes sense given where we came from — people who "once were not a people" and "were shown no mercy" but now have received it.
elements.questionHint: The identity titles are followed by the words "so that" — what specific mission does that phrase introduce as the reason for the identity?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> and has appointed us as a kingdom, as priests serving his God and Father – to him be the glory and the power for ever and ever! Amen.

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This brief verse says Christ "has appointed us as a kingdom, as priests serving his God and Father." Our royal priesthood identity here is directly tied to service — we are priests who serve God and Father — and the whole verse ends not in self-focus but in worship: "to him be the glory and the power for ever and ever." Being made a kingdom of priests points our mission toward serving God and giving him glory, rather than toward status for its own sake.
elements.questionHint: The verse names two things we've been appointed as — what are they, and what does the verse say we do as the second one?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> And now, if you will diligently listen to me and keep my covenant, then you will be my special possession out of all the nations, for all the earth is mine, <sup>6</sup> and you will be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you will speak to the Israelites.”

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God tells Israel that if they listen and keep his covenant, they'll be his "special possession out of all the nations," even though "all the earth is mine" — meaning this priesthood identity is a particular calling within a wider ownership. They're to become "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." This is the Old Testament root of the royal priesthood language Peter later uses — a people set apart, in relationship to a God who claims the whole earth, given a mission tied to obedience to his covenant.
elements.questionHint: God says "all the earth is mine" right before calling Israel his "special possession" — what does that combination suggest about why they were chosen out of everyone else?

elements.text: We are called to embody God’s presence in the world. We are called to make him known, bridging the gap between heaven and earth. We are called to proclaim the good news of reconciliation to all creation and to serve as representatives of His kingdom in everyday life.

elements.text:
Case Study 14b - Hannah

Hannah needs to know that she already has a place in the body of Christ. The body of Christ is made up of many members, and each is vital to the whole. Hannah may feel like a spectator, but in reality, she is an indispensable part of Christ’s body, simply by virtue of her faith in Christ. Her feelings don’t change the truth that she belongs. Hannah’s life is intertwined with the lives of other believers. She is connected to the church in a deep, spiritual way, even when she doesn’t feel it.

There are different possible reasons why Hannah is struggling to connect. The problem might be (mostly) on her side. Perhaps she hasn’t fully embraced the idea that being part of the body of Christ means active participation, not just passive attendance. She could explore how her gifts can serve the body. Or it might be that she hasn’t taken the time (or doesn’t know how) to develop genuine, Christ-centred relationships where she and others can encourage and strengthen one another. Hannah could make progress by joining a small group or inviting a fellow church member for a meal. Building meaningful relationships takes time, but as Hannah invests in her church community, she will begin to see how those connections deepen her sense of belonging. As she shifts her focus to actively participating and serving, Hannah will likely experience the joy that comes from living out her calling as a member of Christ’s body. By serving others, she will begin to see how God uses her to bless the church and fulfil His mission in the world.

It is also worth acknowledging that the problems may be less (or, at least, not completely) on Hannah’s side. Some church communities are structured in a way that makes it hard for at least some people to integrate well. Perhaps the church community is not very good at integrating newcomers, or single people, or couples without children, or older people, or foreigners, or those from a different background to everyone else. Problems like this are not always easy to see, and nor are they quick to fix (and Hannah may not be in a position to fix them). It is never a good idea to jump to the conclusion that the problem in a situation lies wholly (or mostly) with someone else, and not with us, although it is worth Hannah being aware that in some circumstances a church community may not be structured in such a way that it can easily accommodate and integrate people like her. Being a member of the body of Christ is both a gift and a responsibility. It is a gift both to the individuals and the community, and a responsibility upon both the individuals and the community.

Case Study 15 - David (early 30s)

David is passionate about his faith and actively involved in his church. He attends Bible studies, volunteers regularly, and leads a small group. On Sundays, David feels close to God and is encouraged by his identity in Christ. But when Monday comes, and he returns to work, that sense of identity fades.

David works as a marketing manager for a large company. The working environment is competitive and high-pressure. His colleagues often use underhanded tactics to get ahead, and there is a strong emphasis on success and performance. David struggles to live out his faith. He finds himself cutting corners, exaggerating results, sometimes telling outright falsehoods, and going along with office gossip just to fit in and avoid conflict. By the end of the working week, David feels drained and guilty, knowing that he isn’t living as the person God has called him to be.

David wants to be the same person at work as he is at church, but he feels stuck. He wonders, ‘How can I live out who I am in Christ, in a place where success seems to come at the cost of integrity?’ He wonders if it is even possible to reflect Christ in his actions when everyone else is playing by different rules.

Living out who we are in Christ means letting our identity inform our actions. We are called to reflect His love in every aspect of our lives.
Tim Chester

The way we live reflects what we believe about God. If we truly understand our identity in Christ, it will overflow into our daily lives.
John Piper

You were made for a mission. When you live out your identity in Christ, you begin to fulfill the purpose for which you were created.
Rick Warren

elements.text: The Christian life is about embodying the values of the kingdom of God in our everyday lives. We uncover who we are in Christ through our actions. You must choose to live out who you are in Christ. It is a daily decision to trust Him, no matter what the circumstances.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Don’t be afraid, for I am with you! Don’t be frightened, for I am your God! I strengthen you – yes, I help you – yes, I uphold you with my saving right hand!

elements.question: What can help us trust God, no matter the circumstances?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks directly and repeatedly to fear: "Don't be afraid... Don't be frightened," grounding the command in who he is and what he does — "I am your God! I strengthen you... I help you... I uphold you with my saving right hand!" What helps us trust God isn't a technique but this repeated, personal assurance of his presence and active help — his strengthening, helping, and upholding — that meets our fear directly rather than dismissing it.
elements.questionHint: God gives three specific actions he promises to do for you (strengthen, help, uphold) — how might remembering those specific promises change the way you face a frightening circumstance?

elements.text: The Christian life is a process. We grow in our faith, we reflect Christ more and more in our lives, we learn to walk as he walked.

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The phrase "walk in newness of life" comes right out of this verse's picture of having "been buried with him through baptism into death," so that "just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life." To walk in newness of life means our ongoing, daily way of living is meant to correspond to resurrection — not a return to the old buried life, but an actual walking pattern shaped by the same power that raised Christ.
elements.questionHint: The verse connects our "new life" to something that happened to Christ "through the glory of the Father" — what was that event, and how does it become the pattern for how we're meant to walk?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> But I say, live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh. <sup>17</sup> For the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh, for these are in opposition to each other, so that you cannot do what you want. <sup>18</sup> But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul frames walking in newness of life as walking "by the Spirit," which results in not carrying out "the desires of the flesh." He's honest about the ongoing tension — "the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh... so that you cannot do what you want" — but promises that "if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." Walking in newness of life means being actively led by the Spirit through a real, ongoing conflict, not living free of struggle altogether.
elements.questionHint: Paul says the flesh and Spirit are "opposed to each other" — what does he say happens instead when you are specifically "led by the Spirit"?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> You were taught with reference to your former way of life to lay aside the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires, <sup>23</sup> to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, <sup>24</sup> and to put on the new man who has been created in God’s image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Walking in newness of life here involves an active sequence: laying aside "the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires," being "renewed in the spirit of your mind," and putting on "the new man who has been created in God's image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth." It isn't a one-time event but an ongoing process — one that touches how we think as much as how we act, moving us away from deceit and corruption toward a righteousness rooted in truth.
elements.questionHint: This passage names three steps — laying aside, being renewed, and putting on — which step deals specifically with "the spirit of your mind"?

elements.text: Living out our identity in Christ means integrating that identity into our thoughts and actions. To be the kind of people God wants us to be, we must reflect His character in our lives.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> but, like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves in all of your conduct, <sup>16</sup> for it is written, “ You shall be holy , because I am holy .”

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter grounds the call to holiness directly in God's own character: "like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves in all of your conduct," quoting the command "You shall be holy, because I am holy." Personal holiness reflects our new identity because it's meant to resemble the very God who called us — not an arbitrary standard, but a family likeness. Being holy "in all of your conduct" means this isn't confined to select moments but is meant to characterize the whole of how we live.
elements.questionHint: Peter says to be holy "like" someone specific — who is that, and what does imitating that person's holiness suggest about our new identity as his children?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, <sup>13</sup> bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if someone happens to have a complaint against anyone else. Just as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also forgive others. <sup>14</sup> And to all these virtues add love, which is the perfect bond.

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul roots this call in identity first — "as the elect of God, holy and dearly loved" — before listing what to put on: "a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience," along with "bearing with one another and forgiving one another... just as the Lord has forgiven you." Then "add love, which is the perfect bond." Personal holiness reflects our new identity by working outward from who we already are — chosen and loved — into concrete relational virtues, especially a forgiveness that mirrors the forgiveness we've received.
elements.questionHint: Paul says to forgive others "just as" someone forgave you — whose forgiveness is the model, and what does that model suggest about the kind of holiness expected of us?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Therefore, since we have these promises, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that could defile the body and the spirit, and thus accomplish holiness out of reverence for God.

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls believers, on the basis of "these promises," to "cleanse ourselves from everything that could defile the body and the spirit," so as to "accomplish holiness out of reverence for God." Personal holiness here reflects our new identity as people who already possess God's promises — the cleansing isn't done to earn something, but flows from reverence for the God whose promises we already hold, touching the whole person, body and spirit together.
elements.questionHint: Paul says this cleansing is "out of reverence for God" and based on "these promises" already given — what does that ordering (promise first, then holiness) tell you about the motive behind it?

elements.text: The gospel is not just about what we believe, but also about how we live. Being who we are in Christ means leaving our comfort zones and sharing His love. Our lives should display that we are in Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, <sup>23</sup> gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul lists the "fruit of the Spirit" as a single cluster — "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control" — noting "against such things there is no law." Bearing this fruit as part of our new identity means these qualities grow out of the Spirit's presence in us rather than being manufactured by willpower or rule-keeping. Notably it's called "fruit," singular, suggesting these traits belong together as one organic outgrowth of the Spirit's life in us, not a checklist to master separately.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls this list "fruit" (singular) rather than "fruits" — what might that word choice suggest about whether these qualities grow separately or together?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Remain in me, and I will remain in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. <sup>5</sup> “I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in me – and I in him – bears much fruit, because apart from me you can accomplish nothing.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes fruit-bearing entirely dependent on connection: "Remain in me, and I will remain in you... apart from me you can accomplish nothing." Using the vine and branches image, he says a branch "cannot bear fruit by itself" unless it "remains in the vine." Bearing fruit as part of our new identity isn't something we produce through effort separated from Christ — it happens only through ongoing, abiding connection to him, "the vine," with fruitfulness as the natural overflow of remaining attached to him.
elements.questionHint: Jesus repeats the phrase "remain in me" — what does he say happens to a branch that tries to bear fruit without staying connected to the vine?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> for you were at one time darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of the light – <sup>9</sup> for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth – <sup>10</sup> trying to learn what is pleasing to the Lord.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul contrasts past and present: "you were at one time darkness, but now you are light in the Lord," and follows with a command: "Walk as children of the light." He defines the fruit that light produces: "all goodness, righteousness, and truth," paired with the ongoing aim of "learn[ing] what is pleasing to the Lord." Bearing this fruit as part of our new identity means living consistently with what we now are — light, not darkness — letting that identity produce goodness, righteousness, and truth as we keep discerning what pleases God.
elements.questionHint: Paul says believers "were" darkness but "now" are light — what specific fruit does he say this new identity as light is supposed to produce?

elements.text: As we live out our identity in Christ, as His body, we become the hands and feet of Jesus, bringing His love and compassion into our communities. We engage with the world around us, sharing His truth and love in practical ways.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> For we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The answer here is good works, but framed by identity: "we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them." What else we're to do is walk in these specific good works — not works we dream up ourselves, but ones God already planned for us before we ever got there, simply because he made us, in Christ, for exactly that purpose.
elements.questionHint: The verse says these good works were "prepared beforehand" by God — what does that timing tell you about whose plan we're stepping into when we do them?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people, <sup>24</sup> because you know that you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward. Serve the Lord Christ.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reframes ordinary work with a wide scope — "whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm" — and a different audience: "as to the Lord and not for people." What else we're to do is bring this wholehearted, Lord-directed attitude into everything, motivated by "your inheritance from the Lord as the reward," summed up in the simple charge, "Serve the Lord Christ." Even routine tasks become an act of service to Christ himself when done this way.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts working "as to the Lord" with working "for people" — how might remembering who you're really working for change your enthusiasm for an ordinary task?

elements.passageText: <sup>58</sup> So then, dear brothers and sisters, be firm. Do not be moved! Always be outstanding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's charge is to steadiness and effort: "be firm. Do not be moved! Always be outstanding in the work of the Lord." What else we're to do is persist in that work, and he gives the reason we can: "your labor is not in vain in the Lord." Because our labor has guaranteed meaning in Christ, we're freed to keep going with full effort rather than wondering whether any of it actually matters.
elements.questionHint: Paul gives a reason at the end of the verse for why we can keep laboring without giving up — what does he say our labor "is not," when done "in the Lord"?

elements.text: Our new identity in Christ calls us to a new way of living - one marked by grace, love, fellowship, humility, and service to others.

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> His master answered, ‘Well done, good and faithful slave! You have been faithful in a few things. I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master.’

elements.question: What can we look forward to, as we live out who we are?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The master's words to the faithful servant paint the picture: "Well done, good and faithful slave! You have been faithful in a few things. I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master." What we look forward to is this commendation and welcome — recognition for faithfulness, entrusted with greater responsibility, and invited into the master's own joy. It's a future where present faithfulness, even in small things, leads to greater trust and shared joy with Christ himself.
elements.questionHint: The master gives the servant two rewards for faithfulness in "a few things" — what are they, and what does the phrase "enter into the joy of your master" suggest about the nature of that reward?

elements.text:
Case Study 15b - David being who he is

David needs to be shaped by the truth that his identity in Christ is constant, no matter his environment. Whether he’s in church or at work, he is a new creation in Christ. His identity doesn’t change based on his surroundings. God calls us to be holy in all areas of life, reflecting His character wherever we go. David’s work environment may tempt him to compromise his values, but his identity in Christ means that he is called to something greater. He is a child of God in all situations.

David’s struggle to live out his identity in Christ at work is understandable - he faces real pressures. But God promises to be with us and strengthen us, even in difficult circumstances. David doesn’t have to face these challenges alone; he can rely on God’s strength to help him stand firm in his identity, even when it’s hard. David can begin to trust that God’s plan for his life includes integrity and faithfulness, even if it doesn’t seem to lead to immediate success by the world’s standards. By trusting God, David can choose to act with honesty and love, knowing that his ultimate reward comes from God, not from his boss or colleagues.

For David, this might mean making small but significant changes in how he interacts with his colleagues. Instead of going along with office gossip, he could choose to speak words that build others up. Instead of cutting corners to meet deadlines, he can commit to doing his work with integrity, trusting that God will honour his faithfulness. God has prepared good works for us to do, and that includes the work we do in our daily lives. David’s job is not just a means to an end - it’s part of his mission as a follower of Christ. By seeing his work as an opportunity to reflect Christ’s love, David can find renewed purpose.

Instead of viewing his workplace as a battleground where he has to compromise to survive, David can see it as a mission field where he is called to be the hands and feet of Jesus. David can shine the light of Christ in a place where it may not be readily visible. David is not responsible for how others respond to that light. Some may be drawn to find out more, others may be provoked to oppose the light. Some people may be intrigued by the difference in how he lives, others may respond with resistance, criticism or even open hostility. If David lives out who he is in Christ, it may help his career, or it may hinder it. He might get promoted because of his integrity, or he might get fired because of it. It is not David’s responsibility to control those outcomes. His responsibility is simple: to be who he is in Christ.

paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
